subtasks.note: Live. Real recorded sound in place of the 8-bit beeps, a spinner on the right orbit that used to pay nothing, and STARDUST FRENZY — 22 seconds where the whole table pays 10x. Every ball now ends on a bonus counting up. 10-19: you said it was buggy and kind of sucked, so I measured what you actually see. The table was using 71% of a desktop screen and 58% of a phone — a small object in the middle of a room — and on a desktop the buttons sat right on the drain, hiding the one spot you watch when you lose the ball. It fills the screen now (96% desktop, 94% sideways, 72% phone), and it works turned sideways, which it did not before. On a phone: hold anywhere on the table to launch, then tap the left or right half to flip. The table also tells you the trick it never mentioned — hold a flipper to trap the ball, then shoot. That is how you aim at the ramp. And it pays now — there was no payout for pinball at all, so a game into the millions earned you nothing. A go is one coin like every other machine, and beating 500,000 pays tickets. The nightly check that was supposed to catch that turned out to be blind to the whole tavern; it isn't now, and it says the pool table and the dartboard still pay nothing.

subtasks.text: Pool balls need numbers and to actually look like pool balls
subtasks.note: Live. The striped balls had their colour band running the wrong way round the ball, so racked up they showed as a white ball with a wedge down one side. The numbers were there but the white circle was half again too big, so it covered the top of every ball like cream. Both fixed, and every ball has a shine on it now — flat colour was why they read as beads.

subtasks.text: The pool cue is half the size it should be
subtasks.note: Live. Measured: the balls on that table are deliberately a third bigger than real so you can tell a striped one apart from across the room, but the cue was left at a real cue's size. It came to 20 ball-widths long where a real cue is 26. It is 26 now, and the cue leaning on the table matches it.

subtasks.text: Jukebox: touch up the floating music notes
subtasks.note: Live. There were no music notes anywhere in the arcade — the only thing floating near a jukebox was the sparkle round the big one's star, which is probably what you saw. Real notes now rise out of both jukeboxes. The one in the bar also got rebuilt: bubble tubes down its corners and a record turning behind the glass.

subtasks.text: More detail on the bar and the pool table
subtasks.note: Live. Bar: a rack of wine glasses hanging over the counter, a tip jar, a towel over the rail, peanuts, a cut lemon, napkins. Table: brass trim round the apron, brackets at every leg, a maker's badge, leather pocket nets instead of wooden cups, two more chalk cubes and the triangle hung on the side.

mainPoints.title: Bowling island
mainPoints.insight: The main idea is good. Inside the alley is fine for now.

subtasks.text: The demo ball crashes the pins every ~5 s — loud and annoying when you stand there; find a better way
subtasks.note: It is an attract loop now: stand on the island and the lane finishes its ball, then goes quiet — full rack, ball parked, nothing moving. Only one ball in three is a strike (the rest get no cheer), the cycle is 17–23 s instead of 11, and the sound is loudest out on the carpet, not where you stand.

subtasks.text: Make the demo lane look better
subtasks.note: Pin deck with its ten spots, gutters cut as real channels with a steel lip, the neon lying in the oil, an approach with dots, a raised ball return you can watch the ball ride home on — and a sweep rake that wipes the leftover pins into the pit.

subtasks.text: The ball rack and the shoes need a lot more work
subtasks.note: The rack is a two-tier stand now (legs, shelves, chrome cradles, lit fascia, six balls with their finger holes) instead of a trough of marbles. The shoes are half again bigger on a plinth, with a real arch, a dark throat, tongue, laces and a stamped size.

mainPoints.title: Slab City — tutorial & trick progression
mainPoints.insight: A wall of controls is overwhelming. Teach the basics first, unlock tricks by levelling. A bigger park comes later.

subtasks.text: A tutorial that walks through the basics of skating, not a wall of controls
subtasks.note: Six steps, one line at a time in the panel: get on, roll, steer, push, ollie, kickflip. Each one waits until you actually do it. There is a skip. REWRITTEN 10-28 after a two-model read of the whole park: three of the six were teaching people to fail. Step 2 said hold the roll key and step 6 said flick it, so your thumb was still holding it at the jump and the flick could never read — every step that needs the hand off it now says so first, and on a phone it says which thumb. The ollie step marked itself off in the air instead of on the landing. The kickflip step read your save file, so anyone who had ever landed one had it ticked before they read it. And if you bailed mid-lesson, the line kept telling you to push while you lay on the concrete with the board 10 m away — being down now takes the line and tells you to press R.

subtasks.text: An "Open Trick Book" button showing the tricks you have learned so far
subtasks.note: The old wall of controls is shut on every device. One chip now: OPEN TRICK BOOK · LVL 1. Open, it shows a level bar, the moves you have, and the levels ahead.

subtasks.text: Levels that unlock tricks (Skate 3 style: coffin, flips as higher-level moves) and parts of the park
subtasks.note: Eight levels, ROOKIE to PRO, each opening a trick that was dead until then. The COFFIN is in at level 7 — Q with S held, lie flat and roll. I did NOT lock parts of the park, on purpose: see the report.

subtasks.text: Keep it multiplayer: skate around with others to level up
subtasks.note: XP is every combo you bank, so a session with friends levels you the same as skating alone. Two-player check green.

subtasks.text: A stray skating sound plays in the lobby — music, or a leak from the skate park? Find out
subtasks.note: Fixed properly 10-28, after you reported it again. The 10-16 fix only made the little ghost board quieter — the real fault was that its rolling sound had no off switch once you walked through the door, so it played on everywhere for the rest of your visit, and a new one piled on every trip in. One thing now turns all skate sound on and off, every frame, so leaving by any door, opening a menu, or switching tabs all go silent. Checked by reading the actual sound output, on the phone and the desk.

subtasks.text: Later: grow the park once tricks and basics are in

mainPoints.title: Toy Fury — lobby island & toy house

subtasks.text: Island track: gaps at the turns; cars clip into the track and each other
subtasks.note: Each piece of road was a straight box turned onto the corner, so every joint on a turn left a third of a metre of daylight. The road is one continuous ribbon now. And the straight coming out of the loop ran right under the loop's own lower half with a foot of headroom, so cars drove through it every lap — the loop corkscrews now and the two straights are nearly three metres apart.

subtasks.text: Cars clip through the loop-de-loop and fall out of it
subtasks.note: A toy car is stiff and that loop is tight: laid flat on it, the axles sit seven centimetres under the road and the nose and tail nearly twenty. Each car now rides a touch proud of the surface by exactly that amount, only where the road curves up into it — so the flat corners are untouched.

subtasks.text: The toy decorations around the track need a lot more work
subtasks.note: Three scenes instead of scattered props: a pit lane with three numbered garages, spare shells on stands, tyre stacks and lap boards; a grandstand that went from three bears to nine on four rows under a striped canopy; and giant crayons, so you can tell the whole circuit is lying on a bedroom floor.

subtasks.text: The carpet in the main area of the house is broken and clipping
subtasks.note: Every rug was a flat box sitting at exactly the same height as the one under it, so the two fought over which one you could see — the red and yellow edges came out as a crawling stair-step. A rug laid on another sits a little higher now, the way a real one does.

subtasks.text: Clipping in almost every room — objects inside objects; build it with more intention
subtasks.note: Started with the worst one, in the room you named: the sofa was four boxes all inside each other — both arms were buried completely inside the seat cushion, and the back went 18 cm into both. It is five pieces now, each one sitting on or beside the last and none of them inside another. The cat and the cushions were re-seated to match.

subtasks.text: The small things in every room: the ones hanging in mid-air and the ones standing inside a wall
subtasks.note: SHIPPED 2026-10-29, live on the site. Twenty of them. Every curtain in the house hung 2 cm below its own pole — all twelve. The book on the study armchair was left 10 cm in the air when the chair was lowered onto the floor last week. The nine party flags in the kitchen hung from nothing at all; they have a string now. The kitchen apron and the whole bathroom mirror were inside the wall trim, the kitchen bin 16 cm inside the skirting. Also the car's wing mirrors, the shop sign, the window-seat cushion, three coats, a shelf box, the bike seat and the playroom apple.

subtasks.text: The mini tracks in the house should look like the real race tracks
subtasks.note: They were a flat orange noodle in one colour. Now each one is the real thing in miniature: a cream channel with the road banded in two oranges and a blue joiner every fifth piece, posts holding up the high bits, a start gantry with green lights. It costs nothing extra — the long straights are built as one piece of track instead of nine.

subtasks.text: Shrinking down into a track looks buggy
subtasks.note: Found it by filming all fourteen frames of it, which nobody had ever done. Your arms and legs never knew the body had shrunk, so a thumb-sized astronaut kept full-length limbs and folded into a blob with one arm out like a plank. The whole body shrinks together now. It also used to spin you 260 degrees on the way down, so you landed facing backwards; it turns a quarter and stops, looking down the track.

subtasks.text: Everything on the eight little race tracks floats above its own mat
subtasks.note: SHIPPED 2026-10-29, live on the site. Every one of the eight miniatures stood exactly 2 cm off the mat it sits on — the road, the posts holding it up, all the little clutter, the start gantry and the cars. Two centimetres is the whole height of most of those little pieces, and the track's side rail is open underneath, so the gap let you see up inside it. One number: the mats were built ending 2 cm lower than the height the tracks are laid at, in the same commit that first built the house, and the two had never matched. The mats came up to meet the tracks rather than the tracks going down, because the porch track's rail hangs 1.4 cm below the floor line and dropping it would have buried the road in the mat instead. 242 floating pieces down to 52. Worth saying plainly: the check that was supposed to catch this had the 2 cm written into it as normal, in a comment describing the fault exactly — so it reported everything fine for ten days. The rest of the 52 are pieces standing on the track itself, which that sweep cannot see at all; filed, not guessed at.

mainPoints.title: Toy Fury — race revamp
mainPoints.insight: "There's a lot of potential for this game but it just feels like I'm not even really racing."

subtasks.text: Driving: you bounce wall to wall and cannot hold the middle — make it feel like real racing, not just W + A/D
subtasks.note: The car never straightened itself: let go of a key and it kept crabbing into a wall. It eases back down the road now. Time spent scraping a rail went from a fifth of the race to one part in seventy; corners got harder to pay for it.

subtasks.text: Drop the track picker after you already chose a track (offer mode / race type instead)
subtasks.note: All eight tracks had been sitting open on the title screen permanently — the button that was meant to hide them never worked. Fixed, and once a track is chosen the race type and field are what the screen offers.

subtasks.text: Booster pads look like car-wash wipers — redesign them
subtasks.note: They were two upright brushes you drove between. Now the rollers lie across the track like treadmill drums and turn forward, with an arrow on the road.

subtasks.text: Wrecks and explosions should be a big part of it — your car can blow up and die
subtasks.note: Nothing could ever blow up before — fifteen races, zero damage. Now there is a fireball, black smoke, a shockwave that shoves whoever is near, and a car trails smoke when it is one hit from scrap.

subtasks.text: The game looks low resolution — find the cause
subtasks.note: Found it: in the arcade the game drew three quarters of the width of your screen and the shell stretched it. It draws every pixel now, at the same frame rate.

subtasks.text: A brand new player's first race, and saying the overtake out loud
subtasks.note: Live 10-27. Three things. First, your call: someone opening Toy Fury for the first time now gets one gentle race — toy boxes, the easy field, starting near the front — and the two choice buttons are off that screen entirely, so there is one thing to press. They come back the moment that race starts, set to Surprise Me, and they never go away again. Second, the overtake. Taking a place off somebody is the best thing that happens in a race and the game said nothing about it — the number in the corner just quietly changed. It now says PASSED TUNA, with a sound, right beside the number, and it only says it when you genuinely went past someone — not when a rival blew up or dropped out, which also moves your number. Third, two real faults found while checking the first one: today's derby was not the same race for everyone after all (your difficulty button was secretly changing the derby's cars and your starting slot, while the screen said everyone gets the same field), and tapping TODAY'S DERBY from another room has, since the 22nd, dumped you into an ordinary race in the right room instead of the derby — your coin spent, the race you asked for never run. Both fixed, both now checked. Also: the grid card had started naming a difficulty the race had not actually dealt.

mainPoints.title: Toy Fury — car collection
mainPoints.insight: Hot Wheels: collect cars, race the cars you own, spend tickets on cars.

subtasks.text: Design many more car models — spend real time on car design
subtasks.note: Ten rides, live: a dune buggy, a pickup with a real open bed, a delivery van, a chopped hot rod with a blower through the bonnet, and a wedge with a huge wing.

subtasks.text: Collect cars and race the ones you own
subtasks.note: Buy with tickets, keep it until it breaks. The garage now says 3/10 in the garage so the collection counts.

subtasks.text: Showroom: a motorcycle is upside down; one car already has a driver in it
subtasks.note: Your own character now sits in every ride on the shelf. A wrecked bike lies on its side instead of upside down.

subtasks.text: Wheels turn weirdly and some do not attach to the car; car parts clip
subtasks.note: Turning wheels no longer tip over, the kart's front wheels are on a real axle, the bike has forks and a swingarm, and the racing stripe lies on the paint.

subtasks.text: Three cars under the win-rate floor; the ride table was only ever measured on 1 of the 8 rooms
subtasks.note: Measured all eight rooms this time, 960 races a car. The three cars named were fine once the other seven rooms counted — those numbers came from the house, which is the hardest room of the eight. The car that was actually broken was the 120-ticket Rally Pup: it won less often than the free kart, so your first purchase made you worse. It is now the quickest cheap car in a straight line and wins more than the kart. Second thing the eight-room run turned up: each car is strongest in a particular room, by a mile — the Carpet V8 wins 20 races in the garage and 1 in the bathroom. The garage card now tells you where each car wins, and stars it on the day the derby is in that room.

mainPoints.title: Multiplayer — every game
mainPoints.insight: "You're thinking of it from a very narrow lens." Think through the whole party, not one match.

subtasks.text: Pick sides: choose who is on which team
subtasks.note: Live 10-18. Sit at a team cabinet in a room and you get a SIDE A / SIDE B button, so two friends can be on the same team instead of being dealt opposite each other. It turned out not to be a job for each game at all: every one of them already works out teams from the order people sat down, so the room just hands the seats out in the order you asked for. Four cabinets so far — Splatflag, Ice Hockey, Dodgeball and Second Wind — and the button only appears where the game can actually obey it. One thing it does on its own: if you both pick the same side AND bots are off, one of you is moved across before the match starts, because a side with nobody in it is not a game. You see that happen on the button rather than finding out in the yard.

subtasks.text: Team sizes beyond 2v2 where the game allows (3v3, 4v4)
subtasks.note: Live 10-18, and "where the game allows" is doing real work here. Ice Hockey plays 3v3 AND 4v4 — the rink is wide enough for eight and both are formats real hockey plays. Splatflag and Dodgeball go to 3v3 and stop: the Splatflag courtyards are only clear for three a side, and a fourth would stand up inside a wall; the Dodgeball court is 26 across, so a fourth would be shoulder to shoulder with nowhere to dodge. Second Wind stays 2v2 on purpose — going down to become your partner's ambush needs a partner. The host picks the size at the cabinet and it is written on the board and the prompt, so nobody sits down to a different match than they agreed to.

subtasks.text: "Play again" pulls every player back in
subtasks.note: A match ends and both players get a PLAY AGAIN card instead of being dumped in the room. Pressing it sits you back at the same cabinet at the same stake, the card names who else came back, and two presses start a new match. Live, in every party game that reports its ending.

subtasks.text: The host chooses whether to fill with bots
subtasks.note: Live 10-18. BOTS or LEAVE EMPTY, next to the stake at the cabinet, host only. Left empty, the spare seats come out rather than standing there — four friends in a 3v3 play 2v2, not two people against four ghosts. The switch only shows on cabinets that can honour it, which is the point: it would otherwise have appeared on all thirty-odd party machines and changed nothing on most of them.

subtasks.text: Knocked out or finished early: spectate and choose who to watch (Toy Fury, Space Golf), never get thrown to the lobby
subtasks.note: Both games he named are live. Toy Fury: wreck or finish and the board waits — the camera cuts to a car still running, an arrow each way picks who, your result sits over it, and it ends when the last friend is done. Space Golf: hole out first and the card offers WATCH MIKE — the scorecard swaps for the chase camera on your friend, CARD puts it back, and it ends when they hole out.

subtasks.text: Bots wear skins
subtasks.note: Live 10-18. Bots in a party now wear real skins off the shop — a different one each, with its own name — instead of being team-coloured mannequins. The room deals the outfits once and sends them, so everybody's screen dresses the same bot the same way, and because they come off the live shop list, a skin you add tomorrow walks onto the floor as a bot with no game touched. A friend who leaves mid-match leaves a body behind that plays on in that seat's outfit rather than reverting to a blank. One real catch found and fixed: the shop list only loaded when somebody opened the shop, so every bot would have shipped undressed — opening a room fetches it now.

subtasks.text: Cabinets clip a lot, especially the screens
subtasks.note: Live. They were 2.5 m apart and the wide ones are 2.3 m across, so neighbours overlapped in every row. 3 m now.

subtasks.text: Clean up the cabinets; the hall is a giant box — give it a real vibe
subtasks.note: Live. Each room has its own low ceiling, carpet, a lit sign slung over every row, and posters up the walls. The old one was 7.5 m of black void over a 2 m machine.

subtasks.text: Split it: a single-player room and a multiplayer room
subtasks.note: Live. A foyer with two lit doorways: THE SOLO ROW (11 machines, cyan) and THE VERSUS FLOOR (25 with a seat for a friend, pink).

subtasks.text: The Splatflag cabinet picture still shows the old map
subtasks.note: Live. The old picture was from September, four days before the yard was rebuilt. Retaken mid-match.

subtasks.text: One room, not two — the cabinets and the five machines together
subtasks.note: Live. The games room had zero cabinets in 16 m of bare carpet; everything else was crammed next door. Now one floor: cabinets in rows down the middle, skee ball and the hoop left, the claw and the pusher right, air hockey at the end of the lit path. One wide door instead of two — on a phone you used to land facing a blank wall.

subtasks.text: Air hockey: the mallet trails your finger
subtasks.note: Live. Your mallet walked to where you pointed at 3.2 m/s — up to a third of a second behind your hand, every move. It goes where your hand is now: 12 m/s, seven frames down to two, measured on both builds with the same probe. The keys never had the problem, which is why every existing test passed on the bad version.

subtasks.text: The claw looks cheap — spheres in a row in a grey box
subtasks.note: Live. Two things: every prize was drawn facing exactly the same way on a neat grid, and the cabinet had no back, sides or roof at all — you were looking through the glass at the room behind it. The pile is tumbled now and the inside is a lit purple box. A grab still wins a prize the same way; nothing about the game changed, only what you see.

subtasks.text: Skee ball — you couldn't see past your own head
subtasks.note: Live. Your own figure stood dead centre between the camera and the lane, so you couldn't see the ball, the lane or the board. It isn't drawn while you're standing at the lane now. Raising the camera was the obvious fix and was wrong — it tilts down at the same time and pushes the board off the top of the screen.

subtasks.text: None of the five machines pays a ticket
subtasks.note: Live for the three you named. A go at air hockey, skee ball or the claw now costs one coin like every cabinet, and winning pays tickets — 8 for beating the house to seven, 4 for a plush or for rolling 300 at skee, plus the usual 3 every go pays win or lose. Signed out, you still play free and win nothing. The hoop and the coin pusher are still free and still pay nothing; I left them out on purpose rather than add a payout nothing calls.

subtasks.text: Air hockey felt dead — nothing on the table reacted
subtasks.note: Live. The mallet squashes when it strikes, harder the harder you hit; the puck stretches into a streak at speed so you can follow it; it flares as it crosses the line. Your own head was also sitting over your own goal — it steps out of shot now, same as skee ball.

subtasks.text: The hoop and the coin pusher paid nothing either
subtasks.note: Live. All five machines take a coin and pay now. Beat 24 at the hoop, or push more than 25 coins back out at the pusher. The pusher is no longer endless free play — that was a loophole once winning pays tickets.

subtasks.text: The looks still left: skee's lane, the claw's grabber
subtasks.note: Live, all three. The lane is seven maple boards with seams now instead of one orange plank, darkening toward the top where the ring box shades it. The claw is a claw: a hooked three-talon grabber on an amber hub — and it hangs where you can see it, because it used to park under the roof liner and read as four pixels. The chute is a real hole with a lit rim, not a pink slab painted on the floor; a won prize used to sink straight through it.

subtasks.text: Walk in and nothing tells a stranger which machine to try first
subtasks.note: Live 10-27. The wall you face through the archway now has HANGTIME, RIPOSTE and OUT OF THE SUN standing together under one wide lit sign that says START HERE and names all three, readable from the doorway on a phone. Walk up to any machine and it tells you what the game IS, not just what it is called — '2v2 streetball to 11', 'a 1v1 duel, first to 4', 'a dogfight in waves'. Two things turned up that were nothing to do with this job. Every lit sign stuck on a wall in the arcade is tipped forward so you can read it without looking up, and the tip swings its own bottom half INTO the wall — so each of them has been showing its big name and hiding the line underneath it. The sign over the archway is supposed to read 'every machine, and five you play on the floor' and that sentence has been inside the plaster since the 18th. All of them read in full now. And the middle of that end wall, straight down the lit runner, is a strip nobody can ever see: the four machines you play on the floor stand back-to-back against a tall divider on exactly that line, and from the door it blots out half a metre of wall at any height. The first version of the sign went in the middle, as asked, and the divider ate 'START HER|E'. The three machines sit one pace to the left of the runner instead, in clear air. Last one: a machine's walk-up line is written in short pieces so a phone can stack them, and a piece too long to fit is not wrapped, it is simply cut off under the Play button. Blend In has been saying 'needs a friend in your' and losing the rest. Swept all 25 machines; that was the only other one.

mainPoints.title: Coins & tickets — find the balance
mainPoints.insight: One coin a game; 100 tickets buys a skin spin. People should be able to spend pretty normally.

subtasks.text: Check daily coins actually refill (a vault note says claim_coins has never paid)
subtasks.note: They refill. The old note is out of date — it was fixed on 10-08 and has paid 462 coins since. Checked again on the live site: five hours away paid ten coins, and a second ask paid nothing.

subtasks.text: 1 coin per game
subtasks.note: Live. Every machine is one coin (it was 1, 2 or 3). Blend In is still free — it needs a friend and has no bots to beat — and the Undercroft door is free, its contracts take the coin.

subtasks.text: Vs friends: players put tickets up against each other
subtasks.note: It already worked, but 16 of the 20 matches ever played were still holding 595 tickets: the refund only ran if someone asked for it, and nobody did once the room broke up. The arcade asks on arrival now, so stuck stakes come back.

subtasks.text: Vs bots: the ticket payout scales with bot level
subtasks.note: Live, and wider: easy 4, normal 8, hard 16, brutal 30 (was 2/4/8/15). A win under 20 seconds now pays nothing — the ladder was collectable with no game played at all.

subtasks.text: Balance payouts against the 100-ticket spin — lower the spin or raise payouts
subtasks.note: Raised the payouts; the spin stays at 100. 64% of rounds ever sold never paid anything because nothing settled them when you walked out — fixed first, since no number matters if nobody collects it. Every finished round now pays 3 win or lose. An average player reaches a spin in 23 minutes of play (it was 110).

subtasks.text: A cooler map: lean hard into the cartoony look, with outlines
subtasks.note: Live. Warm cartoon asteroid instead of a flat purple plate, pebbles and teal crystals. The outlines were doubled here on 10-15 and that part was wrong -- see the outline line below, 10-29.

subtasks.text: Keep the falling-apart map
subtasks.note: Live. Same rings, bigger fall: the slab about to go sags and glows red-hot, and the one that drops throws dust.

subtasks.text: Bots come in wearing skins
subtasks.note: Live. Nine real shop skins, dealt fresh each match, each bot under its own name.

subtasks.text: You can fly back INTO the island
subtasks.note: Live 10-29. The rock was a flat plate with nothing underneath it -- the game only ever asked whether there was floor at your feet, so a jetpack climbing from below went straight up through the slab, through the boulders hanging under it, and out the top, and for about a second you were inside the asteroid. It is a solid body now, the shape you can see: five metres deep in the middle, two at the rim. Come up underneath it and you slide along the underside and out to the edge instead of stopping dead, which matters, because stopping dead under the middle would hover you there until the tank ran out -- a worse way to die than the bug. Holes a slab has fallen out of are still open: you can fly up through those, and that is the only way through. Proved by throwing a man off the rock four hundred times and watching every single frame of the climb back: nobody was ever inside it. The same check with the underside removed again finds him inside the rock seventeen hundred times, so the check can fail. And it caught something I would never have found by reading: my first version of the fix told you to climb straight up before coming in, which sounds careful and quietly cost a THIRD of every rescue in the game and halved the length of a round. That is out. Rescues and round length are now exactly where they were before I touched it.

subtasks.text: The outline on the character is way too thick
subtasks.note: Live 10-29. You were right and it was measurable: this was the only game in the arcade wearing an extra thickness multiplier on top of the one the lobby uses, so its thickest lines were drawing nearly DOUBLE the lobby's -- twelve pixels against seven on a desk screen. A note from 10-15 had doubled it on the reasoning that the line was too thin on a phone, and that reasoning was simply wrong about how the line is sized. It is back to exactly what the lobby draws. Measured rather than eyeballed, by rendering the same frame twice, once with the outline and once without, so the pixels that changed ARE the line. Side by side with the old shots the difference is obvious: every pebble used to sit in a soft dark smudge, and now it has a clean line round it and the rock reads brighter.

subtasks.text: Some of the sound effects are just not good
subtasks.note: Live 10-29. Four named and swapped, all from our own recorded kit. The SHOVE was a boxing slap for a moment that throws a grown astronaut off a cliff -- it is now four layers inside a twentieth of a second: the weight lands first, the crack on top, the suit rattles, and the man it happened to makes a noise. The FALL was one short whoosh, so the whole point of the game went past in a sixth of a second -- now you hear him cry out and the sound drops away below you. FLYING BACK ON, the best thing that happens in this game, had no sound at all -- boots, suit, and a bell, and the bell is only for yours, or a rock full of eight people scrambling back turns into a wind chime. And the WINS were backwards: every single round played the full match fanfare, three or four times a match, while actually winning the whole match was silent. The round gets a short sting and a bit of crowd now; the match keeps the fanfare. Checked by logging what actually PLAYED, not what the code asked for: fifteen real recordings, no leftover beeps.

subtasks.text: When you get shoved off, you can't see yourself fall or fly back
subtasks.note: Live 10-29. The camera only ever watched the people still standing, and it always looked at the same spot a little below the floor. So the moment you were knocked over the edge you left your own picture: you fell fourteen metres and died, or you flew all the way back, with your body off the bottom of the screen the whole time -- the best thing in this game, happening where you could not watch it. Now, while you are off the rock and still alive, the shot becomes the fall. It drops with you, tilts DOWN toward the horizon so a fall looks like a fall instead of a dot sliding about under a map, and backs off as far as you are thrown -- never closer, because how far from the rock you are is the whole point. It eases in just under the height where a lucky grab still saves you, so a clutch save never jerks the camera. The first version framed the whole rock and left you a speck in the corner, so it frames the GAP instead: you, the edge you left, and the rock behind it. Checked on a desk and on a phone, at five points of a real knock-off, on a fall and on a flight back -- you are on screen in all of them and so is the edge. And the slab you left now throws dust off the spot you were standing on, whether you were shoved off it or it dropped out from under you. Finished on a PHONE 10-29: that first pass was right on a desk and only half right on a phone. A shove throws you sideways about as far as it throws you down, so the fall ran diagonally -- and a phone is narrow. The rock slid off the side of the screen the whole way down and you were about the size of a grain of rice. The camera now TURNS while you fall, so it ends up looking straight in along the line you were thrown: the rock sits directly above you, the fall runs down the tall screen, and the width is free. You are three times bigger, the rock stays in the picture at every depth, and the desk shot got better too. The turn is the risky part -- a camera that spins makes people feel sick -- so it is governed to a slow sweep and it unwinds as you fly back up. And I found one thing a still photograph could never have shown: for the first third of a second of every knock-off, on a real fall, you were already off the edge of the screen while the camera was still looking at the empty arena. Where the camera POINTS now grabs you the moment you pass the rim, before any of the rest of it moves.

subtasks.text: On a phone the fighters are specks and half the screen is empty sky
subtasks.note: Live 10-29. Measuring the fall fix printed this by accident and it was worse than the thing being fixed: during the actual match a man was a FORTIETH of the screen tall on a phone, where the same moment on a desk gave you six times that. So the one second of dying was three times clearer than the ninety-nine seconds of fighting that caused it. The cause is arithmetic, and the old note in the code had it backwards. A phone is more than twice as tall as it is wide, and the camera was framing the whole round rock -- which means fitting it across the NARROW way. That fixes the camera twenty-six metres out, and then the tall direction has twice the room it needs and spends it on black sky, top and bottom. On top of that the lens was standing almost straight up over the rock, and a man seen from straight above is squashed to half his height before distance even gets to him. The old zoom could never have fixed either: it moved the camera up and back by the same amount, which cannot change the angle you are looking from. So the camera now comes in to sixteen metres and looks ACROSS the fight instead of down at the floor. A fighter went from a fortieth of the screen to a fifteenth, and every single frame of being knocked off -- which is the part you watch -- is now big enough to read, where the first half-second of it used to be a speck jammed against the edge. The desk got slightly better too, and the camera actually swings LESS than before. What it costs: the left and right of the rim are now off the screen. I took that on purpose -- the rim is scenery, the man about to shove you is not -- but the one thing it could have ruined is seeing which slabs are left while the rock falls apart, so I built a check that projects every remaining slab and insists you can see every one you could step onto. It immediately caught a real one: late in a round, with the rock down to its middle and everyone bunched up, the camera pulled in so close that a live slab four metres away was off the edge. There is now a floor under how close it will ever come. Two fixes in this came from the camera being photographed MOVING rather than posed -- the posed shots were all green while a real shove still threw you off the side for a frame, because the camera was being told you had moved by your position, which is always late. It reads the shove itself now. Found and left: another fighter can still be clipped at the side with his name tag cut in half; that wants the tag pinned to the edge, and it is filed.

subtasks.text: Still choppy next to the lobby, and a friend's own body is the rawest thing on screen
subtasks.note: Live 10-30. You were right, and it was not the frame rate. The lobby moves your character every time it draws a picture. This game worked out where everybody was sixty times a second and then drew them only at those sixty spots -- so on a fast screen one picture in eleven showed two steps' worth of movement and the other ten showed one. Measured on a 165Hz screen, your body moved either the full distance or none at all, picture to picture. It now draws you part-way between the last two steps, so every picture moves you the same amount: dead even, on a 60Hz screen, a 144 and a 165. The worse half was on a friend's screen. Everyone ELSE was already being smoothed out -- and YOUR OWN body, the one thing you are actually watching, was the one left raw. That is fixed the same way, and I checked with two real browsers in one room that a shove still lands exactly where the host says it does: a quarter of a metre at worst, and the game never once had to yank you back. I also told the room that this game now draws between its steps, so a later job can let it run at the lobby's full speed. One more thing I only found by LOOKING at the phone picture afterwards: every fighter's name was being printed twice -- eight names on a rock with four people on it -- with the ghost copy stuck wherever that fighter was standing when the line-up last changed. Four names, four fighters now. And two of this game's own tests had quietly been wrong for weeks: one never pressed the button an invite link has asked for since the 18th, the other still expected Escape to dump you straight out instead of opening the way-out menu you asked for. Both fixed, and I proved each one on a game I had not touched before believing it.

mainPoints.title: Sideways
mainPoints.insight: A fun single-player start; it belongs in the single-player room.

subtasks.text: The engine revving sound is annoying — rework it
subtasks.note: live 10-15 — it has gears now, so the note drops instead of climbing forever; quiet on a straight, roars when you drift. The siren came down with it.

mainPoints.title: Ice Hockey — make it fun
mainPoints.insight: "I don't want to remove the game. I just want to see how we can make the game better."

subtasks.text: The loop is grab puck, skate to goal, shoot, repeat — deep dive on what would make it fun
subtasks.note: LIVE. Measured 14 matches: from in close you scored 0 of 44, while a long shot scored 15% — the game paid you to hang back and fire, which is the loop you described. Close shots now pay best, and holding the steal button is a lunge that strips him but floors you if you miss.

subtasks.text: Charging a shot looks goofy — make the stick swing look natural
subtasks.note: LIVE. The stick was swinging right round sideways with the blade two metres in the air, and it held there while you glided. It loads back and low now, both hands on it, shoulders turned, and whips through the puck.

subtasks.text: The camera is cooked and the movement is super choppy
subtasks.note: LIVE. Two separate faults, both real. One: the game thinks in fixed steps sixty times a second, and it was drawing you at the newest step and nothing in between — so on a fast screen one frame in eleven showed twice as much travel as the other ten, five times a second. It now draws you part-way between steps, and a skater at a constant speed moves exactly the same distance every frame, measured at 60, 144 and 165 — with a deliberately broken version run first to prove the measurement can fail. Two: every bit of the camera's smoothing was applied once per frame drawn rather than per second, so the camera behaved differently on every screen; the same play now draws the same camera path at 55 and at 82.5 frames a second, to within 1.3%. And after a goal the camera used to slide the whole length of the rink to the face-off — it cuts now, in one frame, on your screen and on a friend's. Three more things fell out of it: on a friend's screen a saved shot could briefly be drawn going INTO the net before snapping back, because the guest was guessing the puck forward past the keeper with no keeper in its copy — it now stops at the goal line and waits for the host to rule; other players snapped about 28 degrees at a time as they turned, and now turn; and the game was drawing 78% more pixels on a phone than its neighbours do, for a picture nobody can see at arm's length. 3v3 and 4v4 were the other half: with more than two a side, two players both read themselves as the one chasing the puck, every supporter ran to the same spot, every defender marked the same man, and EVERY pass in the match — yours included — went to the same teammate. Each one has a job of its own now, and the two-a-side game is untouched, proved identical across five seeded matches against the old build.

subtasks.text: Needs a better name — propose three
subtasks.note: LIVE. You picked BARN BURNER on 10-29 and it now reads that way everywhere inside the game — the tab, the title card, the result. The folder, the link and your saved tutorial flag are deliberately unchanged, so nothing you have already played forgets you.

subtasks.text: Four plays you choose, and a shootout when it's level
subtasks.note: LIVE. Four decisions where there used to be one. PASS: a ring shows which mate gets it, and the pass now leads him — a pass travels more than twice as fast as a skater, so it used to land six strides behind the man and he turned to chase his own pass. Passes that connect went from 60% to 88%. The bots used to pass ONCE in a three-minute match, which is exactly the 'same thing over and over' you described; they move it up the ice now, about twelve times a match. SHOT: hold the stick left or right while you wind up and the puck goes inside THAT post, no assist — shown as a target in the net and on the phone button. DEKE: a button of its own (Q on a desk, a pad under your right thumb on a phone) slides the puck across your body, past his stick; it costs a quarter of your speed for a quarter of a second, and he can still poke it off you while it moves. REBOUND: saves bounce out live here — one in six leads to another shot — and nobody was ever there, so after every shot one mate drives the far post and gets there in about a third of a second. And a level match no longer plays another two-minute period: it goes to a SHOOTOUT, three five-second attempts a side, one skater against the keeper. The first-visit card teaches the three plays. A shootout that stays level ends the match tied — whether that should refund the coin is yours to call.

mainPoints.title: Broadside Bay (pirate ship) — pivot
mainPoints.insight: Start small, sink ships, grow. No screens that pause the game.

subtasks.text: Start in a small boat; every ship you sink grows yours
subtasks.note: LIVE. Five hulls, launch to ship of the line, swapped on the water mid-fight. Your FIRST kill promotes you.

subtasks.text: Multiplayer: battle other ships to become the biggest (agar.io feel)
subtasks.note: LIVE. Both captains now start in a little launch and the fight grows you: every plank you knock off her makes your own ship bigger, mid-fight, no pause. Her rung rides her name tag so you can see who is ahead. Still two players, not a lobby of ten -- say the word if you want more seats.

subtasks.text: Levels from kills upgrade durability, firepower and cannonball capacity
subtasks.note: LIVE. Hull, ball damage and guns a side (= balls per volley). Big ones are slower and turn worse.

subtasks.text: Remove the pause-the-game picks (powder monkeys, chain shot, rum ration)
subtasks.note: LIVE. The whole deck is gone, and the pause with it. Chain and grape went too (they were cards).

subtasks.text: Remove pressing E to walk around the ship
subtasks.note: LIVE. One station: you never leave the wheel. Space fires the side that bears.

subtasks.text: Keep waves in single-player; aiming can improve later
subtasks.note: LIVE. Waves untouched; the King's ships now work up against your rating instead of your cards.

subtasks.text: A stranger's first cabinet opened on a wall of text (from the blind-stranger run)
subtasks.note: Live 10-17, and all three measured against the old build on the same machine. One: the opening screen made you read 324 characters on 13 lines - over half an upright phone - before you were allowed to touch anything, and three of those blocks were the controls the how-to-play card already teaches one at a time. Your first voyage now reads 90 characters on 3 lines; the full screen comes back on your second run, when the words mean something. Two: the how-to-play card stuck on step 2 for both strangers, for 30 seconds, because that step was waiting for a King's ship to drift into your gun line - something you cannot make happen. It now moves on when you do the thing it asks. A thumb that only ever does what the card says reached the last card in 3 runs of 3, against 1 of 3 before. Three: both strangers said dragging to steer 'did not obviously do anything', and the reason was the camera - it swings toward the nearest ship, and that swing was cancelling three quarters of your turn out of the picture. It gives most of it back while the wheel is over, and there is a HELM bar at the bottom now that moves the instant your thumb does and names the side. Start a run and drag sideways.

mainPoints.title: Hangtime — touch-ups
mainPoints.insight: "Otherwise I think this is a fun game."

subtasks.text: A better map: lose the odd background audience and the extra court rings — keep only the 3-point line
subtasks.note: The crowd is a rock ridge now. Only the 3-point line is painted on the floor, and the orange dunk circle retires once you have dunked — it was a hint that never switched off.

subtasks.text: Dunking from behind the basket goes through the backboard — block it
subtasks.note: The backboard is solid now. Fixed where your feet are held, so shots and passes stop going through it too.

subtasks.text: A swish sound on a clean 3
subtasks.note: It was already playing — the crowd roar started on the same instant and buried it. The net goes first now, and a deep 3 snaps.

subtasks.text: Backing up for a 3 sometimes forces a moon dunk instead
subtasks.note: The button said STEPBACK while the game ran a moon dunk. Both now read one rule: backing up is never a dunk.

subtasks.text: "Dash in the air to reach it" did nothing, and POSTERIZED printed on top of a player's name
subtasks.note: Live 10-18. Two things the last Hangtime pass wrote down and left. The game has been telling you to dash in the air to reach a pass since the move shipped, and it bought you no extra reach at all -- only a dash along the ground did. I measured it before touching anything: a leaping player reached exactly as far as one standing still doing nothing. Now a dash in the air reaches just as far as one on the floor, and the button says PICK while you are off the ground instead of going blank. It is still something you have to DO -- jumping without kicking at the ball takes nothing, which I checked, and the computer players don't use it, so the move is yours and the game plays the same otherwise. Second: on a wide screen, when you dunked on someone, the big red POSTERIZED landed directly on top of YOUR OWN floating name -- a grey tag with half its letters poking out of the word. Names under the banner now fade out of the way for the two seconds it is up. An upright phone was never affected, and I left it alone there. Jump at a pass between the two bots -- that is the move that was dead.

subtasks.text: On a phone, a callout like SHOOK HIM was drawn on top of the word HANGTIME and neither could be read
subtasks.note: Live 10-21. It was written up as two callouts stacking on top of each other while one faded. It was not that, and it could not have been: this game has exactly one callout on screen at a time, and a new one replaces the old rather than sitting under it. The other word was the court's own name, PAINTED ON THE FLOOR -- so of course it never faded. On a phone the callout drops to the lower part of the screen, and the note in the code explaining why says it goes there because the near floor is empty. The near floor was not empty. The court's name was lying on it. I tried moving one of the two out of the other's way first and measured it properly before giving up on it: the camera zooms in and out as you play, which slides anything painted on the floor about 150 pixels up and down through a strip of screen only 70 pixels tall. Held upright the word wants to be high, held sideways it wants to be low, and there is no spot that is safe in both. A word on the floor cannot dodge a word on the glass, so only one of them stays a word -- the name has come off the floor. The soft glow it was sitting in stays, so the floor still does not read as a hole, and I looked at before-and-after pictures of that patch of court to be sure. Two more while I was in there: the callout now sits on its own soft shadow, so it stays readable over players and the backboard as well; and a callout that happened to fire during the tip-off countdown used to get stuck 22% of the screen too high for its whole life, which is fixed. Play a match on your phone and shake a defender -- the word is alone on the floor now.

subtasks.text: The AI just spams dunking all the time, and a friend sees the game choppier than you do
subtasks.note: Live 10-30, in five pieces. THE DUNK SPAM: the computer decided to drive on a coin flip BEFORE it ever looked at whether a jump shot was wide open, so the drive took about 88% of possessions whatever was in front of it. It now prices every option -- drive, jumper, moon dunk, lob -- and takes the best one, and it drops a drive when help arrives. It will never turn down a genuinely free dunk, because that is the move you liked. Measured with a stand-in player in the game: dunks were 48% of everything the bots scored and are now 34%. THE OTHER HALF of the same problem: nothing in the game punished a drive, because your own team-mate never left the floor -- every jump in the defending code sat behind a line that only ever ran for the man guarding the ball, and a defender with his feet down cannot block at all. Your mate now rotates over and goes up with you: a stand-in's dunks got met in the air 43% of the time before and 68% now. And a bot's dunk no longer takes the whole screen -- it keeps its sound and its explosion but loses the side camera, the slow motion and the freeze. Yours keeps all of it. A FRIEND'S SCREEN: the game was sending the host's clock and the SHOT clock under the same name, and the shot clock won -- so your friend was smoothing everybody's movement against a number that counts down from 12 and jumps back to 12 every time somebody catches the ball. That is the whole stutter, and the freeze after a basket. Also fixed: the court froze for the host and kept running for the friend on every block and steal, so your own body slid about a metre when the host caught up; the ring that shows you where to jump to deny a dunk never appeared on a friend's screen at all; and RUN IT BACK did nothing in a room opened from a link. THE FEEL: the shot verdict counted frames instead of time, so GREEN sat up for 1.18s on a slow phone and 0.79s on a fast one -- it is 1.1s on both now. The thumb stick had no dead zone, so a thumb resting on the glass crept your man forward. Stances spring now instead of snapping. NEW -- THE ALLEY-OOP, which you asked for by name: pass while your mate is in the air near the rim and he catches it and dunks it. Works both ways -- you lob to your bot mate, and he lobs to you when you go up. It can be picked off on the way and blocked at the rim like anything else, and it pays 2. There is a real cut now too: when the man guarding your mate turns to help on the ball, your mate goes to the rim. THE MAP: a parked rover, supply crates and two empty scaffold stands, all outside the lines so they never get in the way of the play -- and no crowd, which stays gone. There is a SECOND court now with identical rules, and RUN IT BACK swaps between them. The backboard finally has its shooter's square, which is the one marking in basketball you actually aim at. One thing I could not do: your skin's aura still does not show in this game, because the shared piece that draws it does not exist yet -- that is filed as its own job.

subtasks.text: Stop asking for a name — use the player's name; signed-out players get "Player 1"
subtasks.note: live 10-15 — the name box is gone; signed out you are Player 1, in a room Player 1-4

subtasks.text: The camera is "bugged" (Zack, 2026-10-29)
subtasks.note: 10-29 LIVE. The shake was the bug and it was one bug, not seven: a hit or a catch did not shake the lens, it threw it to a brand-new random spot 55 to 165 times a second, and it read as a glitch rather than a punch. It is one smooth shove now, the same one in both views. Second, picking RED put the camera on the far side of the court and then FLEW it there over the first second of the round, straight through the gym and across its own look point — the court appeared to flip over. It starts where it belongs now: 5.7 units of travel measured before, under 2.0 after. Third, a catch zooms in on the catch instead of on whatever happened to be in the middle of the screen. And if you are on the bench the camera watches YOU on your rock, not the patch of floor you were knocked down on. Proved across 24 replays — red and blue, upright and sideways, all six seats — with zero faults.

subtasks.text: A 3v3 room loses two players: nobody in seats 5 or 6 is drawn, and throwing from one kills the frame
subtasks.note: 10-29 LIVE. Found while fixing the camera. The room lets a host pick 3 a side and the game seats all six, but the drawing code stopped at four: anyone in the last two seats was invisible — no body, no ring, no shadow, no name — and if YOU were in one of them, throwing a comet killed the whole picture. The game swallowed the error silently, which is why it had never been reported. Six of everything now, each with its own bench rock, and seats an ordinary 2v2 does not use stay hidden instead of standing at the middle of the court.

subtasks.text: It is choppy next to the lobby — "it's a fixed camera, sure, but then it has smooth movement like the lobby?" (Zack, 2026-10-29)
subtasks.note: 10-29 LIVE. The game thinks 60 times a second and your screen draws 55 or 165 times, so every body stood still for a frame and then jumped two steps. It draws between its steps now — and not just the players: their rings, shadows, name tags, the comet in the hand and the aim line out of it, all together, because moving only the body would have left the rest sliding off it. Measured on three different screen speeds: under 2% variation in how far anything moves per frame, and the test still fails if the fix is switched off. The other half only bites in a room: everybody except you was frozen for four frames at a time and then teleported, because your friend's body was only ever moved when a packet arrived. Now it keeps moving between packets and the packet eases it in. Checked with two real games talking to each other.

subtasks.text: "I wish there was more of a power system to it where if you threw the ball harder it would be harder for the other person to catch. I can kind of charge up a shot more" (Zack, 2026-10-29)
subtasks.note: 10-29 LIVE. Half of this already existed and NOTHING drew it: holding the button for half a second took the comet from 23 to 47 and cut the time to catch it from 260ms to 110 — the one thing you could feel was the one thing you could not see. There is a meter in the throw button now, and a bar on the desk, with a mark where the ordinary charge stops. The comet carries its power in flight too: a soft one is a dull pebble, a hard one is a white-hot comet with a fat tail, and there is a ring that snaps out of your hand when you let go. Then the part you asked for: KEEP HOLDING past full and it says OVERLOAD — 0.65s more for 54, and 90ms to catch. No hold time anywhere is slower or easier to catch than it was, which is the rule I built it to. 90ms is a deliberate floor: your friend's catch is judged on the host's screen and their press arrives up to 50ms late, so anything tighter is a throw a friend simply cannot catch. One thing that surprised me: the bots could not feel ANY of it, because they aimed their catch at the window itself — a number no player can see — so a harder throw just made them press later. Fixed; measured over 1200 throws a band.

subtasks.text: The ball has stars on it — give it a real soccer-ball pattern
subtasks.note: live 10-15

mainPoints.title: DodgeFall — both screens must agree, or the game goes
mainPoints.insight: "If we can't figure it out then it's pointless and we'll have to remove the game."

subtasks.text: Deep dive on lag compensation: a kill must be obvious on BOTH screens
subtasks.note: live 10-15 — it was never the internet. The screen drew a body at one angle and the game judged it at another; when someone changed pose the game tested a body a hand's width from the one you aimed at. One angle now, and a kill finally has a thump when playing with friends.

subtasks.text: If it cannot be solved, removing the game is his call
subtasks.note: decision

subtasks.text: Freezes when you are about to reach the final green
subtasks.note: Touching the green ran the rest of the field to its finish in one frame — up to 106 seconds of dead page, worst on the long holes. Spread across frames now: worst stall 0.12 s. Live.

subtasks.text: The camera gets stuck — sometimes you cannot look up or where you want
subtasks.note: A touch the browser steals left the VIEW button HELD, so the camera stayed locked 21 m overhead. All five buttons let go now, and alt-tab does too. Live.

subtasks.text: "Sometimes going faster and sometimes I'm not going faster when I'm in the air"
subtasks.note: A long empty flight was secretly running 3x fast, and the speed-up itself ran off your frame rate. Gone: one speed in the air, the same at 55 and 120 frames a second. Live.

subtasks.text: "There should be a cooldown before you instantly throw your club at someone"
subtasks.note: Nothing can be thrown for the first 5 seconds of a hole, a throw now takes a moment to wind up that you can see and hear coming, and 80 degrees of turning away calls it off. Rivals obey all of it, including their own 8 second rest. Live.

subtasks.text: "It just seems so gloomy... this game is so quiet, like nothing's going on"
subtasks.note: Brighter on every hole (measured: 37% to 42% lightness, a third more of the screen above mid-grey). Finishing a hole makes a sound for the first time — the fanfare was in a branch the game could never reach. Plus a trail in your own colours, wind while you fly, and music. Live.

subtasks.text: "Spectate the people once you finish, then you all get pulled into the next lobby"
subtasks.note: Finish first in a party and you are put over your friend's shoulder with no button pressed; everyone starts the next hole together, measured at 91-144 ms apart on two real browsers; and the last hole ends for everybody with nobody pressing anything. Solo never waits for bots. Live.

subtasks.text: "The bots suck"
subtasks.note: Measured, and he was right: they failed to finish 1 run in 8 on the long holes. Now 1 in 27. They also swing where you can see it, brake coming in, smack themselves back instead of blinking, walk on their own legs and start fights. Live.

subtasks.text: Three holes a coin
subtasks.note: A go is three curated holes now, not all nine. Three sets on the front screen, each about five minutes, each with its own target. One coin at the door, one payout at the end. Live.

subtasks.note: Live 10-17. The case now says what one costs and where tickets come from -- 100 tickets, every round pays 3, a hard bot up to 30 -- and the greyed-out button is a working 'Make a free account' instead.

subtasks.text: The first cabinet a stranger reaches (Broadside Bay) opens on a wall of orders/text before you can touch anything
subtasks.note: Fixed and live 10-17; re-checked on the real site 10-18 -- a maiden voyage reads 3 short lines, not 13, and all 32 checks pass on phone and desk.

subtasks.text: Broadside Bay: the 'How to play 2 of 4' card sits over the ship and never advances under blind taps
subtasks.note: Fixed and live 10-17. Card 2 was waiting on a King's ship a newcomer cannot cause; it clears from the handspike now. Re-checked on the real site 10-18.

subtasks.text: Broadside Bay: dragging to steer isn't obviously doing anything to a new player
subtasks.note: Fixed and live 10-17. The chase camera was subtracting 78% of your own turn out of frame; 33% now, and the wheel has a needle. Re-checked on the real site 10-18.

subtasks.text: Games directory header is clipped on a phone -- title hidden behind the search box, "About" cut off
subtasks.note: Already fixed 10-12, and checked again 10-18 before touching anything rather than taken on trust: the title fits and About sits inside the screen on an upright phone, a sideways phone and the desk. Under 640 px wide the search box takes its own row. Nothing to do.

subtasks.text: Cold load shows a black "Loading the arcade..." card for several seconds, worse on a slow/throttled phone
subtasks.note: Live 10-18. Measured on your real site on a slow phone first: eleven seconds of a card with not one moving pixel, so there was no way to tell a loading arcade from a hung one. Three things were wrong underneath. The arcade was waiting its turn for no reason -- the page finished arriving before the browser even thought to go and fetch the 3D library, so the two queued up instead of coming together; they now come together, and on a phone with decent signal you are in the room in under five seconds. A white "Play from a plain list instead" button was being shown to every single visitor from the first moment, as if the arcade had failed -- it was meant to appear only on a failure and had never worked, because of a rule this file had already patched thirty-five times in other places and never once here. And the card's own timers were counting from the wrong moment: they sat at the very bottom of a very large page, so they started when the browser finished reading, not when you arrived -- a "twelve second" rescue was firing at twenty-two. Over 400 attempts where the player did everything right, it paid the three to 81 in 100 on a computer and 11 in 100 on a phone. The button lied on top of it: it stopped saying MOON DUNK about a fifth of a second before the jump stopped being worth three, so the one thing telling you the move exists went dark while your thumb was still travelling. The payout, the button, the on-court ring and the hint were four separate copies of the same rule and they disagreed. One rule now, held open long enough for a thumb: 11 in 100 becomes 86 in 100 on a phone, 100 in 100 on a computer. Bot play is unchanged, proved line-for-line against the old build on 120 games, with a deliberately-broken copy run first to show the test can actually see this setting.
