subtasks.text: And the big arcade's own card was stale too: it still sent you "left" and "right" through two arches, in a room that has had ONE archway since 22 Oct
subtasks.note: LIVE 10-27 (clone cca3028), read back off the real domain on both a phone and a desk screen. The card now says what is actually there: straight ahead through the archway, cabinets round the walls, the air hockey table down the middle with hoops, skee ball, a claw and a coin pusher behind it. Its heading said "Pick a door" on a card you only ever see AFTER walking through one -- it says "Have a go". The reason this lasted five days is that the check only ever asked whether the word "arch" was in the card, so the stale copy kept it green; it now asks the room how many openings it built and fails if the words disagree. A new walk-through test (down the south carpet, in the coin door, read the card) failed six ways on the old build and is green on the new one.

subtasks.text: The same readers' second list: ten small things inside the big arcade itself
subtasks.note: LIVE 10-27 (clone 00d1240), every one of them re-run on the real domain, phone and desk, plus two real arcades in one room. The four worth knowing: (1) a cabinet that costs coins used to fly you in, load the game, and THEN tell you that you were short -- it tells you at the cabinet now and you never leave the floor. (2) Sit at a game two friends have already filled and your screen said you were seated, for as long as you stood there, and your next press tried to stand you up from a seat you never had. You now get told the table is full, in about half a second. (3) The machine by the foyer door said CHANGE and did nothing at all -- it is a cashier and it opens your purse. (4) A game your friend is sitting at only showed its sign from five metres away, which is close enough to read the machine instead; it now reaches you from across the room, and says 1 / 2 SEATED. Also: the invite link said anyone who opens it lands in the room (they have to tap Join), leaving the round now says you keep that round's tickets, leaving a room puts the Host button back, and a strip of buttons over every game that CSS switched off on 8 Oct is finally gone -- four of our own tests had been quietly reading it, and one of them had been skipping its whole first half for nineteen days. Two things the job sheet got wrong and I changed on the evidence: the seat-sign fix as written would have worked for the host and nobody else, and the title-card nudge as written could push a card further off the screen than it already was -- it now checks whether it helped and puts the card back if it did not.

mainPoints.title: Polish sweep 10-19 -- ten things found on the evidence (c0)
mainPoints.insight: A hint fixed top-centre is on the door: every island’s door sits there, and so does the tour card.

subtasks.text: Toy Fury's toy house: a whole lot of clipping -- objects through the ground, props through the track
subtasks.note: Live 10-19. 275 of the 445 little objects on the eight play mats were hanging in mid-air -- 60 of the garage's 65 -- because building a mat throws away the thin uprights so you can see into it, and a desk leg, a fence post and the side of a bath are all thin uprights. The legs come back now, cut off at whatever they hold. In the race itself: the bed's blanket and pillow floated 4-6 cm over the mattress, the sofa stood on nothing with its feet beside it, and the bathroom climb ran through the folded edge of every towel -- which also wrecked the motorbike on every single run. Queue item 115.

subtasks.text: The mouse-lock pill stood on the door, and behind the tour card for the whole tour
subtasks.note: Live 10-19 16:45 (clone a998750). "Click to lock the mouse" sits beside Controls now and dims after seven seconds. Driven through the real Enter: verify/_polish10/lock-pill.mjs. Queue item 120.

subtasks.text: Bowling: pins clip into the ground, pins need work, and the sweep that takes the fallen ones away (queue 119)
subtasks.note: Live 10-19. You were right and the 10-18 fix only got half of it. I measured every pin's lowest point against the board under it on every frame of 671 balls: 799,605 frames out of 1,298,273 had a pin inside the wood. All ten stood 13 mm down in the maple, always — the lift was right for a pin lying flat and zero for one standing up, so the pins had no feet. It is measured off the board now and is clear at every angle, not just at the two ends: 0 frames out of 1,298,731. Two more came out of the same measuring. Every pin fell BACKWARDS, toward you instead of away — one inverted sign, true since the lane was built. And a pin going over the back edge put its nose half a metre down through the deck. Both fixed. Then the thing you described: STRIKE CITY had no pin machine at all, so the fallen pins blinked out and the next rack blinked in. Now the table comes down and lifts whatever is still standing clear, the rake sweeps the dead wood off the back into the pit, and the table sets your pins back on their spots — or a fresh ten comes down after a strike or a spare. Last: the lane's oil. The game has worked out a real oil pattern since the day it was written and never drawn it, so the hook came off something nobody could see; you can see it now, heaviest down the middle and drying out before the pins. Checked on the live site, desk and phone, over 6,307 frames.

subtasks.text: The tour card covers what it points at, and "Skip the tour" is a 14 px underlined word -- dock it, make Skip a real button
subtasks.note: Live 10-20, phone, desk and sideways. Both strangers lost the room under this card: it was 430 px wide at top centre, which on every screen is where the arcade stands its tall things up. On your phone it now docks low in the empty red carpet, in the only band that is neither the room's signs nor your own character — the big machine's sign reads straight through now, PLAYER 1, 25 GAMES INSIDE, IN THE COIN DOOR, which is the sign that tells you where to go. On a desk it sits down the left, out of the middle. Sideways it goes wider and shorter so it stays clear of the press-to-play bar. "Skip the tour" was an underlined word 85 by 40; it is a proper 44 px button now, the same pill as Controls. The cards also stopped changing size as you go — every one is the same height, and the phone copy is cut to the two lines that fit, which is the third time a stranger has said there are too many words before you get to play. Asking for the key list now puts the card away instead of stacking two panels of the same lesson. The checker that was supposed to be guarding all this had been failing on four counts since 10-18 — it still walked the tour through two steps that were deleted when the carpet route was written. Fixed, and taught to measure the real thing: every card, the prompt at its tallest, and every machine face within 16 m, on all three screens, with a canary that fails the run if the camera reading is stale. SECOND HALF, live 10-20 later the same night: the card still covered one thing, and it was the thing its own last page points at. Your purse — the little chip top left with your coins and tickets, or "Guest, nothing saved" — sits two pixels above where the card was parked, in the same corner, so on a desk and sideways the card sat on all of it for the whole tour while the last card read "Tap your purse, top left". It now docks underneath it, and the chip reads clear on every screen. Your phone was never affected — the card is docked low down there. The checker could not see this because nothing had ever told it the purse exists; it measures it now, and the purse's position is written down once instead of twice, so the next card to move cannot land on it again.

subtasks.text: The game card’s ticket line reads like a price -- say "win 8 tickets", with "1 coin" on its own line
subtasks.note:
SECOND PASS, live 10-20 06:00 — the first pass only fixed four games and I had written down that the rest were fine. They were not. I checked all 36 games in a browser this time instead of by eye, and 25 more were putting the prize and the price on the SAME line: "beat them for 8 tickets · 1 coin". Two numbers side by side, same size, same colour, nothing saying which one leaves your purse — which is the thing you complained about, just in a different shape. All of them now put the coin on its own line underneath, reading "1 coin a go". Two more games had the exact fault I thought I had already fixed — KitchenClash and the Rearview card showed a bare count under each difficulty, and KitchenClash never told you the price at all, so the only number on its card was a prize that looked like a cost. Three games said "1 COINS". And one real bug fell out of the measuring: Best Line was throwing an error on EVERY single load inside the arcade, because the arcade tells a game what it pays while the game is still loading — the same fault that turned up in Riposte yesterday, so it is now a written rule rather than a thing I find twice. One game, Fog Rally, is fixed in the vault but is not on the site at all (it 404s), so there was nothing to ship for it.

AND THE BIGGEST ONE, found because the checker said "I cannot see this game" instead of passing it: the Rearview difficulty buttons have NEVER shown a ticket figure. Not since the game was written. It was asking the arcade for the prizes the wrong way round, so the answer was always empty and every difficulty showed as a bare word with the prize nowhere on the card. All four now read win 4 / 8 / 16 / 30 tickets, live and checked on the real site.

FIRST PASS (10-19): He was right, and it was on four cards, not one: Riposte, Splatflag, Deep Line and the bowling lanes all put a bare number under a difficulty, which is the shape of a price list. They now read "EASY / win 4 tickets", and the coin — the one figure there you actually spend — sits on its own line under the row as "1 coin a bout". Said once, not on all four chips: repeating it is what made the row look like a menu in the first place. Riposte and Splatflag never mentioned the coin at all before. Two things turned up while measuring. Every Riposte load was throwing an error that blanked the difficulty row for a moment, because the arcade tells a game what it pays while the game is still loading — fixed. And the checker itself was blind: it was rendering every game WITHOUT the site's own styling, because the test server was handing stylesheets over as the wrong kind of file and the browser quietly dropped them. That has been true of every headless check in the catalogue, so anything that measured a width or a colour was looking at a page no player has ever seen. One line fixed it for all of them, and this card was re-measured with the real look on.

subtasks.text: The 15 known button-height failures left over from the ticket-line pass -- owed, not excused
subtasks.note:
Live 10-20. Checked all 15 and none of them was a button-height problem. Eight were my own checker: it never answered the game when the game said hello. The real arcade always answers straight away, and Ricochet Tanks waits for that answer before it shows its title card at all -- so under the checker it sat on its black LOADING screen for three seconds while the checker took its measurements through it, and reported four perfectly good difficulty buttons as unpressable, twice. Fixed in the checker; all eight now pass. Fourteen more were the line that says "touch or press anything", which is not a button at all -- it is a hint, and the screen behind it takes the press, which is exactly what the words tell you to do. My checker had no way to tell the difference because it only ever MEASURED buttons. It now presses them, where a thumb would land, and asks the real question: did the game start? All fourteen start the game.

One was real and is now fixed and live: in Last Call, on a laptop-shaped window, the line telling you how to start the game sat off the bottom of the screen. The card is a centred stack, and when a centred stack is taller than the screen it hangs off BOTH ends and you cannot scroll to either one. The big LAST CALL wordmark was sized off the width of the window only, so a wide-but-short laptop got the biggest title in the whole arcade on the shortest screen; it is now capped by height too, which costs the phone nothing and takes 58 pixels off the laptop card. There was already a fix for this on a phone held sideways, written for screens under 500 pixels tall -- which left every laptop between 500 and 700 unchecked, in the gap between two sizes that both passed. A 1366x768 laptop is about 1280x650 and sat right in it. Measured at nine heights from 420 to 900: everything from 620 up now fits, where before 720 itself did not.

The checker is stricter now, not quieter: I deleted the list of 15 excused failures rather than adding to it. Anything hanging off the screen now fails at any size with no exceptions, and everything else gets pressed for a real answer. Still open: Last Call's card is still too tall for a phone held sideways -- that is a different screen and wants its own pass.

subtasks.text: Broadside Bay never tells a FIRST-TIME player that a go costs a coin
subtasks.note:
Live 10-20, checked on the real site on a phone and a desk. Every other game states the price and the prize on its title card. Broadside Bay did too — except on your very first visit, which is the one visit where it matters, because nobody has learned yet that a go costs anything. A pass two weeks ago cut the first-timer's title card right down, on purpose and rightly: it had been five blocks of text on an upright phone before you were allowed to touch the screen, and it is now her name, what she is for, and TAP TO SET SAIL. But the price got swept out with the rest. So a stranger bought their first go for a coin having never been told there was one. The difficulty picker stays hidden — it genuinely means nothing until you have sailed once — and the card gains one quiet line instead: "1 coin a go, beat 4 waves to win 8 tickets". Neither number is invented: the arcade really charges 1 and really pays 8 for that run, and a first voyage is always that difficulty, so what the card says is what the game pays.

THE OTHER ANSWER IS YOURS, and nothing is blocked on it: a first go could be FREE instead, and say so. That is a real option for a stranger wandering in off the portal, but it changes the economy, so I did not help myself to it. The game is honest either way now.

I nearly broke the game outright doing this. The line that paints the price runs about a thousand lines before the switch that knows whether this is your first visit, and the arcade tells a game what it pays while the game is still loading — so reading it from there would have thrown an error on EVERY single load, in the arcade and out. That exact fault has shipped twice this week already (Riposte, Best Line), which is the only reason I looked for it. It is now written down as a rule rather than a thing I keep rediscovering.

And the checker that was supposed to be watching this had never been able to see this game at all. It can now, in both states — first visit and after. Fixing that turned up a fault in the checker itself: it was reading the price line as raw text, which welds two separate lines on screen into one word ("...8 tickets1 coin a go") and stops both numbers matching. It failed a card that was perfectly correct, and the same glue would have hidden a genuinely broken one. That fix covers all five games it watches.

subtasks.text: Toll Bridge tells you a round costs a coin and never once tells you what you win
subtasks.note:
Live 10-20. The arcade does hold real prize figures for this game -- 4 tickets for an easy bridge up to 30 for a brutal one -- so there was nothing to invent, only something to say. Every bridge in the list now carries what that bridge pays, right under the EASY/HARD badge that decides it, and the coin is stated once under the whole list instead of against every row.

The bigger find was the card you get for actually crossing. It said the single word PAID and no number at all -- you could cross and never learn what you won. It now says it: +4 TICKETS.

And a real money bug underneath both. The game works out how hard a bridge is by sending a hundred imaginary strangers across it, which takes a moment, and the bridges you can tap soonest are exactly the ones still being worked out. If you tapped one of those, the arcade charged you and settled the round at 'normal' -- 8 tickets -- no matter what the list went on to say the bridge was worth. So the prize shown and the prize paid could simply differ, in either direction. The bridge is now measured before the coin is taken, so the two always agree -- and tapping a fresh bridge also used to freeze for half a second doing it, now down to a tenth, plus it was showing none of the little markers for where other people died.

One thing for you, not a bug: all six house bridges are EASY. 75-95% of strangers get across every one of them, so the whole floor pays 4 and the 8/16/30 rungs are unreachable on it -- the ladder only wakes up on a nasty bridge somebody builds. I did NOT quote "win 4 to 30" on the card because of it; the line says what is actually on the board and widens by itself when a harder bridge turns up. Whether the house bridges should get meaner is a balance call and yours.

subtasks.text: Out Of The Sun's price-and-prize card was the one card in the arcade nothing could check
subtasks.note: Live 10-20, checked on the real site on a phone and a desk. Every other game writes that card as text, so a machine can read it back and tell us if the wording ever goes wrong. Out Of The Sun paints its card straight onto the picture instead, like a sign painted on a window rather than a label stuck to it -- so the checker could see nothing at all, and said so every run. Two weeks ago somebody looked at it with their own eyes, pronounced it fine, and that was still the only evidence we had. The card now writes down what it painted, in the very same breath that paints it -- which matters, because a note kept off to the side goes stale the first time the wording changes and then quietly reports last month's card forever. This one cannot, there is nothing to keep in step. On top of that the checker reads the actual pixels where the words should be, because the card telling us it painted something is not the same as ink landing on the glass. I proved both halves by breaking the card on purpose twice: once drawing the price in invisible ink, once sneaking in an extra line. The first one slipped past the written-down version completely and was caught only by the pixels. Both were caught, both were put back. The real payoff was immediate and was not this game at all: the new checker's first sweep of all 36 games found that Broadside Bay's first-visit card -- shipped an hour earlier, the very thing on the line above -- had put the price and the prize side by side on one line, which is the exact muddle this whole run of work exists to stop. The player coming back already had it right; the first-timer, the only one who sees that card, got the bad version. Fixed and live. Games the checker is blind to went from three to one, and the one left is a known open question, not a blind spot.

subtasks.text: DodgeFall 3D took your coin and paid you nothing back, and its card never said what a go was worth
subtasks.note:
Live 10-28, proved on the real site while signed in: the cabinet took one coin and paid three tickets for walking out of a round, which is what every other cabinet does and what this one had never done since it opened a month ago. The game itself was never at fault. Each game tells the arcade "a round is starting, at this difficulty" and "the round is over", and DodgeFall has said both since the day it shipped. What was wrong was a single yes/no switch in the price list: with it off, the arcade takes the coin at the door and never writes a receipt, and the thing that pays can only pay against a receipt. So the promise on the cashier's board -- every round pays something -- was simply untrue at this one machine. The switch is on, read back off the live database, and a signed-in round moved the purse both ways: a coin out, and nineteen tickets in for a won hard round.

The same question asked of every other machine found one more in the same state: Lane Day, which is the game our own written guide holds up as the example of a game that pays properly. It was flipped in the same breath. Four other machines that take a coin pay nothing on purpose, because they have no bot to beat, and those were left alone.

The second half is the card. The game owns the EASY/MEDIUM/HARD choice, so the game has to say what the choice is worth, and it did not -- you picked HARD, fought seven opponents that aim where you are going instead of where you are, and found out afterwards. The card now reads "a 5-slice streak wins 16 tickets" under HARD, 8 under MEDIUM, 4 under EASY, with "1 coin a go" on its own line underneath. Those figures are read live from the arcade, never typed into the game, so they cannot drift. Signed out it says "sign in to win tickets" and quotes no number; in a plain browser tab it says nothing at all and the card looks exactly as it did.

One thing worth knowing, not a bug: the arcade's prize ladder actually pays 4 / 8 / 16 / 30, not the 1 / 2 / 5 / 12 written in the original setup file from September. Two of my own test harnesses copied the old numbers out of that file and went green while the real machine paid double. Both now read the live figures and break loudly if the ladder is ever rebalanced again.

mainPoints.title: Every game reviewed 10-21 -- the order to work it
mainPoints.insight: Zack by text: "Do a deep analysis on every single game in the arcade ... the skee ball game just looked terrible. I want everything to be popping, jumping, and shaking." 39 cards, a ranked table and a work order are in Logs/game-manager/deep-dive-2026-10-21-every-game.md; nothing was edited. These are items 1, 2 and 4 of that order, transcribed row by row with the line or shot that found each one. Item 3 (re-apply the stranded Undercroft item 111 build) is deliberately NOT here: a STARTED-and-abandoned build is reported, never resumed by a lane.

subtasks.text: Skee ball: a ball-follow camera, so the landing is not a 90 px postage stamp
subtasks.note: LIVE, verified on the domain. Measured before: the board was 117 px of a 720 px desk frame and 106 px of 844 on a phone -- and the SAME size while aiming, rolling and landing. Now it closes to 474 px (66%) on desk and 405 px (48%) on a phone as the ball drops in. skeeCam() blends from the pose cameraStep() already made toward a follow pose 2.0 m behind the ball and 0.75 m above it, looking at the 50 cup -- blending, not replacing, so aiming is unchanged (119 px before and after) and walking away needs no snap-back. The sim is untouched: skee-check passes 17/17 on desk and phone, same 410 score, and again against the live site. The HUD also had to move: the board now reaches the middle of the frame, where the centred panel covered its near lip and the whole 10 band, so on a wide screen it steps to the left.

subtasks.text: Skee ball: the board answers a score -- the ring you hit lights and bulbs chase for 0.6 s
subtasks.note: LIVE, verified on the domain, desk and phone. The ring you hit fills with its own colour, its number flips dark on the bright fill, and 24 rim bulbs run an every-third chase for 0.6 s. A 100 lights ONLY the pocket the ball entered -- proved by a real corner 100 on the live site (the far pocket stayed at its resting value). A gutter or an over-the-top lights nothing: the board staying dark IS the answer. Painted, not built, so it costs zero draw calls and 0.1 ms a repaint. One find on the way: lighting the 10 region literally fogged the whole face pale, and a 10 is the commonest score -- it now lights a violet band just outside the 20.

subtasks.text: Skee ball: the ball rattles in the cup before it drops, and the score number pops
subtasks.note: LIVE, verified on the domain, desk and phone. A scoring ball now runs the groove it landed in and the groove swallows it -- 2.3 turns for a 50, 3.0 for a corner 100 -- sinking from the board's face to behind the ring box's own front face, so the board cuts the ball and it is gone. The orbit is the ball's OWN arrival speed, so a tight cup whirls and a wide trough makes one lazy lap: the score is in the motion as well as the number. The marquee's points number swells (88 to 134 px of ink, same digits) and COUNTS UP, 10 20 28 35 40 44 48 49 50, with the HUD's number popping alongside it off the same value. A gutter does neither -- the silence is still the answer. Two changes from the plan written here, both deliberate: no bob and no floating +50. A bob at the landing point is still a ball sitting on paint, and a +50 that flies away leaves the number it came from unchanged -- making the score itself climb says the same thing in the place he is already looking. And NO cup geometry: a lip laid on a painted ring would sit on top of the one thing last night's fix lights.

subtasks.text: Skee ball: the power meter is measured straight only, so the 100 corner roll is unreadable
subtasks.note: LIVE, verified on the domain, desk and phone. The bar now re-measures for the angle you are holding, so it describes the roll you are about to make. Mapping the whole aim stick first turned the plan here into something better than three cached sets: the decision is sharper than it looked. Straight, the 50 is open (12% of the bar). Turn off straight and the 50 CLOSES -- it is unreachable at any angle past about a seventh of the stick. The 100 lives in one narrow window around half-stick, where it shows as a bright orange band at the top of the power bar with a white edge, 33 px wide and labelled. Past that window it vanishes again, and at FULL angle the best score on the board is a 40 -- while the game's own hint tells you the 100s are in the corners, which is the lie the old meter could not help telling. Proved by a real roll on the live site: released in the middle of the painted band at the angle held, it scored 100. The hint line now teaches the instrument instead of the controls. Two notes against the plan written here: the band above the 100 is a 10, not a 0 -- over-cooking a corner costs you 90 points, not all of them -- and 37 angle buckets are measured rather than 3, because a sweep costs 2.7 ms on desk and 4.1 ms on a phone, so one is banked per idle frame and by the time you drag there is none left to pay for. Zero extra draw calls; the sim is untouched (skee-check still scores the same 410), and items 139/140/141 all still pass.

subtasks.text: Skee ball: the HUD panel covers the near third of the lane and the ball in hand
subtasks.note:
LIVE, verified on the domain -- phone, phone-sideways and desk, every check passing. Measured before touching anything: the panel was 274 px of a 390x844 screen, 30% of the picture. While you AIM it covers floor, not lane -- but the camera rides the ball, so at the LANDING its top edge sat right over the ring board's near lip and the lane's far end, the one frame where the score is decided. It is now 159 px with the coaching line up and 114 px once you have rolled, and the board's lip is clear. Sideways is the bigger win: 274 px against 390 px of height was 70% of the screen, now 41%. Three things went, none of them shrunk: the title row (the cabinet's own marquee already reads SKEE BALL and the balls counter is right below it), the 'Leave the lane' button (the red LEAVE GAME key top-left is the one way out of a machine and calls exactly the same thing -- the check taps it for real and the go ends), and 30 px of accidental margin -- the message is a

and only blackjack's panel ever zeroed the browser's default, which in this layout does not collapse. The power bar and the big score number were deliberately left full size: they are items 141 and 142's work and they are what the space is for. Found and fixed while looking: the emote face button sat lit and unpressable underneath the panel, because the room's 'am I at a machine' test was a hand-written list that had missed seven machines including this one; it now reads the room's one derived answer, so all twelve machines are fixed and the list cannot go stale again. Zero new draw calls; the sim is untouched (the scripted go still scores the same 410), and items 139/140/141/142 all still pass.

subtasks.text: Every machine panel in the arcade: ten of them stand 30 px taller than they were drawn
subtasks.note: LIVE, checked on the real domain, phone and desk, 240 checks passing. Found while shipping the skee ball panel: its message row cost 98 pixels, and 30 of them were an accident. The status line in these panels is a paragraph, and a browser puts a blank line's worth of space above and below a paragraph unless something says otherwise -- only the blackjack table ever said otherwise. Ten panels had borrowed the same line without it: roulette, darts, the coin pusher, the claw, hoops, air hockey, pool, pinball, the jukebox and bowling. One rule now covers all twelve and two were deleted, so the file is two lines shorter than before. I walked to all ten and opened them the way you would -- stand at the machine, press to play -- and measured every row of every panel as a box on screen, twice each, on a phone and on a desk, and took the picture. That is what changed the fix from 'make it shorter' to something I could prove: the space was not only making the panel tall, it was holding the message 15 pixels off the panel's own spacing, while every other row sat on it. Now all ten sit on the same spacing as their neighbours, each panel is exactly 30 px shorter on both screens, and blackjack and skee ball -- the two that already had the rule -- moved zero, which is how I know nothing else was touched. One more thing fell out of the same three lines: roulette shouts your wins in green and your losses in red, except the colours were written for the blackjack table only, so the one table on the floor that pays real tickets had been printing 'Pays 35, up 170 tickets' in the same grey as an error. Fixed with it. Deliberately NOT changed: on the ten the message is the line that teaches you the game, and it stays full size -- shrinking it to blackjack's small grey would be a different decision, and not one this asked for.

subtasks.text: Hoops: the green band was measured at a still, centred rim you do not have
subtasks.note: LIVE, verified on the domain, desk and phone, every check passing. Same bug as skee ball's meter, one machine over, and worse: the green was measured ONCE, for a hoop standing still and dead centre, and kept for the life of the page -- while you can aim, and for the last 20 seconds the rim slides along its rail. So in the endgame, the part of a go that decides the score, the bar described a hoop that was not there. Mapping the aim/rim plane first changed the fix three times. One: the rim keeps moving THROUGH the flight and through your charge, so simply handing it the rim's position is still wrong by up to 12% of the bar -- the needle is a clock, and each power now flies at its own moment with the rim sliding on. It is measured the instant you press, so the green cannot slide out from under the needle while you read it. Two: 'the widest window' is a chaotic idea once the rim moves -- two shots 20 ms apart would hop the band 8% -- so EVERY window is painted now, the way skee ball's meter already works. Three, and the loudest lie: where nothing could score the old code painted a fixed 8% of green anyway, which is the whole outer third of the aim stick. Now there is no green at all there, and the aiming ring on the backboard turns RED, so the answer is where you are already looking. What it does to the game: at every point in the rim's sweep there is a wide window somewhere on the stick, and the right aim tracks the rim -- so the endgame is a lead-the-rim game and the bar finally says so. Aiming straight at a fast rim scores nothing; leading it opens the widest band in the game, and one line now says so the moment the rim starts moving. The cell sizes were chosen on measured error rather than taste (48 x 18: 2.9% of painted green sits where the ball would not drop, against 12.2% at the first guess), a cell costs 2.5 ms on a phone, and the still-rim set is banked on idle frames so the first 25 seconds never pay for it. Proved by six real endgame shots on the live site, released in the middle of what was PAINTED, at both rim speeds: six baskets.

subtasks.text: Hoops: hideMe was never applied, so your own figure stands in front of the ball
subtasks.note: LIVE on the domain, desk and phone, 26 checks green on each. Worse on a phone than the review said: the helmet filled the lane, the ball in your hands was behind it, and the first third of every shot's arc was hidden -- you could not see your own ball leave. Now you stand at the line looking up it and nothing of you is drawn. The camera was tuned AROUND the figure, so it was re-measured rather than assumed: 15 (distance, pitch) states, each read as pixels -- where the backboard top, the rim, the ball and the cabinet's own front lip land, and how much glass the panel leaves. Nothing beat what is shipped. Closer makes the rim bigger but pushes it under the guest toast at the top of the screen; flatter cuts the dead strip of cabinet at the bottom but shrinks the hoop. So the lens is unchanged on purpose: the figure was the problem, not the framing. Guarded by the page's own answer on open AND after you walk away, with two canaries that each redden only the line they aim at.

subtasks.text: The player shadow draws under every in-hall machine, because it ignores player.visible
subtasks.note: LIVE, shipped in the same build as the hoops one above, because they are the same bug: hiding you at hoops without this would have left the disc behind. It was not theoretical -- the shipped skee ball screenshot has an uncast black oval sitting on the floor in the middle of the frame. Fixed at the one line that writes it rather than at each machine: you are hidden in exactly three places in the whole room and all three mean the same thing. Proved by a canary that puts the old line back and reddens the shadow check alone.

subtasks.text: The coin pusher drops coins onto the plate when the cabinet face is forward
subtasks.note: LIVE on the domain, desk and phone, 22 checks green on each. Timing now matters at the pusher, and it never did before. Drop a coin while the pusher is slid forward under the hole and it lands ON the pusher, where it does nothing at all until the stroke pulls back -- up to about 1.7 seconds of a coin you paid for sitting on chrome. The first thing I did was measure the obvious version of this fix, and it would have changed nothing: the old code dropped your coin 11 cm further forward when the pusher was out, which LOOKED like it rewarded the worst moment, but it paid exactly the same, because the pusher shoves everything behind it back into line within a sixtieth of a second. Where a coin lands is erased instantly; only being somewhere the pusher cannot touch survives. Numbers, over 24 different starting piles: a player who waits for the right half of the stroke gets the same back as before (145% of what they put in, now 144%) and a player who hammers the button as fast as it lets them went from 125% to 102%. So the good line is untouched and only the careless one moved, which is the direction your own review asked for -- it called this machine too easy by name. Three things tell you which half you are in: the marker on the shelf is gold when the hole is clear and turns red and lifts onto the pusher when it is blocked, the DROP button lights up on the same test because on a phone your eyes are on your thumb, and the first time a coin of yours lands on the pusher the machine says so and holds that line for six seconds. Finding my own mistakes: the teach line was being painted over by 'GOLD! +5' a fifth of a second later, and the marker was sitting exactly on top of the coin it points at, hiding it.

subtasks.text: The coin pusher's pile never stacks, never slumps, never avalanches
subtasks.note: LIVE on the domain, desk and phone, 26 checks green on each. Your review said this pile 'never slumps, never stacks, never avalanches' and listed a coin stack as the thing a pusher IS. It has height now. Drop onto a spot the shelf has no room for and your coin lands ON the pile instead of in it, where it pushes nothing -- it just rides. It is carried along by the coins underneath, slipping back a little every stroke, until there is nothing left under it and it drops into the gap it was bridging and shoves the front all at once. That is the avalanche. The thing I had to get right: the pusher face is 6 cm of chrome against a 7 mm coin, so it shoves both layers alike, and if that were the only force a second layer would just be a taller picture of the same machine -- the same trap as the last pusher job. Being carried and slipping is what makes the height actually change what the machine pays. What it does to the money, over 24 starting piles: hammering the button went from 102% of what you put in to 85%, and dropping on the gold marker from 145% to 117% -- but the player who drops ONE coin a stroke never buries the hole, never stacks, and still gets 142%. That is a new skill the machine did not have: do not bury your own drop hole. I also ran five goes back to back on one pile, which is the honest question since this machine keeps its pile between visits, and after the first go everything settles to about break-even either way -- so the big first-go payout your review called too easy was the packed starting pile all along, not the stroke. One yes/no for you below.

subtasks.text: Toy Fury: a hidden host freezes the room, because there is no hidden-host timer
subtasks.note: LIVE, the served file byte-for-byte the one that was tested. Measured against the old build first: a host that put its phone away went to 0 words a second (6.0 while watching), and on the friend's screen its car AND all six of its bots were written off as DROPPED OUT -- and were STILL out when it came back. Now the sim and the word to your friends keep going while the phone is away: the car holds its real road speed (x0.92 of the watched pace), the bots keep theirs, and nobody is written off. NOT host-only, unlike air hockey's version of this: every screen in Toy Fury drives its own car and reports it, so a hidden GUEST froze itself on everyone else's road the same way -- one guard where both route through. Two things the shape needed that air hockey's did not: the sender's clock has to keep moving or every word is thrown away as one already seen, and the touch stick has to be let go on hide or a thumb that was mid-drag drives in circles for the whole minute the phone is gone. The worst case was the garage, where it never recovered at all -- the host is what deals the race, so a pocketed phone left the friend on a greyed-out READY with no 30 s rescue coming; the bench now proves a hidden host still starts a race nobody else readied for. 24 checks in verify/hidden-host.mjs, 13 of them red against the old build. The arcade's own host-hidden-check.mjs could not answer this: it wants four WebGL contexts and cannot get them while the other lane's headless Chrome is up, which is why it had never been pointed at this game.

subtasks.text: DodgeFall 3D: a hidden host freezes the room, because there is no hidden-host timer
subtasks.note: LIVE 10-22. The host's canyon kept running while its tab was hidden: 0 ticks/s before, 54 after. Found a second fault the queue did not know about -- a friend who pockets their phone kept hanging on their rope on everyone's screen for ever, because the sim reuses a player's last input when nothing new arrives and a frozen phone can never send the release. Both fixed. 19 checks green on desk and on a phone.

subtasks.text: The WIN moment has no freeze, flash, kick or number in any game on the floor
subtasks.note: ALL THREE ARE LIVE. COMET CLASH IS LIVE 10-22 (3 of 3), and it is the odd one out: this game ALREADY had the freeze, the flash, the shake and the catch zoom -- the expectation that it did not was wrong, and reading the file first is what caught it. What was broken is that the moment DELETED ITS OWN WORD. One callout shows at a time (right, and deliberate since 10-05), but newest-wins was blind to whether the newest mattered: inside a single catch, with no frame drawn in between, the word CAUGHT! was wiped by its own banner two lines later. Measured over 150 seconds of play, CAUGHT! appeared on ZERO frames -- the biggest, rarest beat in the game said nothing at all, on your screen and your friend's. A near-miss WHIFF half a second after a real hit ate the OUT! too. Callouts carry a rank now, so the chatter gives way to the moment. The THROW RELEASE, which is what the row was actually about, had a sound and a small shake above a hard charge threshold and nothing else; now letting a comet go shoves the lens along the throw, scaled by how long you held it, on YOUR throw only. It does not freeze on purpose -- stopping the game on your own button is how a throw starts feeling like lag. Also fixed on the way: callouts could draw behind the scoreboard (the streak words measured 42-46 px down a 720-tall screen, under a 68 px board), and a guest's body kept walking through a freeze the host was holding, so every single hit rubber-banded them. Found by LOOKING at the shot, not by a check: letting the catch keep its word put the banner straight through it on a desk -- the phone was clean at the same instant, which is why one screen is never the check. The banner steps around it now. 12 checks green, 9 canaries each proving its own check can fail. BROADSIDE BAY IS LIVE 10-22 (2 of 3). Sink a ship and the bay holds still for a beat, goes gold, the lens is shoved at the wreck, and what she was worth floats off her -- a sloop is +1, the flagship is +8. Five sizes, from a ball finding wood up to your own ship growing a rung. And it turned up something worse than the missing moment: ONE LINE OF STYLING went missing on 10-15 and buried a whole layer of the screen -- the '4 of 6 shots hit' grade after every broadside, and the arrow that points at a ship you cannot see. Drawing perfectly, underneath the sea. Every check we own reads that canvas directly, so all of them were green; it took a photograph. 1 of 3 still owed, and it is backlog item 154 (Comet Clash) -- filed there by the 2026-10-22 morning brief because this row CANNOT re-queue itself: polish-chain.ps1:150 only harvests status todo, and :153 then refuses any text already on the backlog in any tag, SHIPPED included. Item 151 shipped game 1 and claimed the next top-up would re-pour this row; it never could. Do not re-open this row to todo -- the dedupe will silently skip it. 2 of 3 done. SKIN KICK IS LIVE 10-22: score and the room stops dead, the screen flashes in your colour, the camera is shoved along the ball's line, and +1 or +2 climbs off the ball while your own score digit punches -- four sizes, from a slide tackle that takes the ball (a blink) up to the goal that wins the match, which also runs 0.8 s in slow motion with the lens pushing in. Checked on the real domain on a phone and a desk, and both screens get it when you play a friend. Two things I had to fix to make it read: the room keeps sweeping after the ball, so a freeze that let the camera keep gliding hid its own kick (the lens is held now), and the number sat 74 px ABOVE the top of the screen because a goal is scored in the net, which is the far, high end of the picture. Next slot: Broadside Bay (it has the most hits a minute on the floor and zero freeze), then the Comet Clash throw release. Found, not fixed: on a PHONE the arcade's own round menu button sits on top of your score digit, so the digit that punches is behind it -- the floating +1 is what you actually read there, and that is a shell problem on every game, not this one.

subtasks.text: Two outside readers went over the shop and the locker line by line (10-27) and found nine things
subtasks.note: EIGHT OF THE NINE ARE LIVE on the real domain. The ninth is copy that only becomes true once the direct-buy shelf exists, so it waits for that build rather than promising a shelf nobody can see yet. What shipped. (1) THE WORST ONE, and it is a stranger's first move: tap a skin you do not own, read 'Get it from a case', press it -- and the whole shop SHUT and threw you at a sign-up form. The case screen, which is where the price, the odds, what a repeat pays back and the 'Make a free account' button all live, was never shown to a visitor at all. Now an unowned skin opens the case for everyone, and the account is asked for by the button that has the reasons standing next to it. (2) 'Open another - 100' stayed pressable with nothing in your purse, and one case is usually all of it, so that was the NORMAL end of a spin. It is dulled now and says what you are short, in the same sentence the case uses everywhere else. (3) An empty case used to say 'You own every skin in the case' -- flattery it could not possibly know, because that list has never once looked at what you own. An empty list means the catalogue did not arrive, so it says the case is shut. Odds that will not load say so instead of showing six dashes. The same check found a real crash underneath: a catalogue that came back EMPTY (not missing) took the whole wardrobe down inside the opening animation, which reads as a shop that just never finishes. (4) If the equip call THREW rather than failing politely -- a dropped wifi, a sleeping phone -- every card and the button went dead for the rest of the session with no message at all. The same trap in the case was worse: it also holds the exit shut, so a dropped connection locked you IN the shop. Both released properly now, and the skin you are given is the one you PRESSED, not whatever your thumb had moved to while it was loading. (5) The reel was 7.9 seconds you could not leave, for a prize the server had already handed over before a single card moved. There is a REVEAL NOW button on it, and a phone set to reduce motion skips it entirely; it stands where Open does, so the phone bar never grows a fourth button. (6) The statue on the plaza rebuilt itself on a 20-second clock wherever you happened to be standing -- a fifth of a second of work on a slow phone, for a figure two rooms away that nobody was looking at. It dresses when you walk in now, and everyone still sees the same one. (7) Dead code, and a see-through blur that was being paid for and then switched off fifteen lines later. (8) Walk to the stand in the first seconds of a cold load and it used to flash 'Accounts are still loading' and refuse to open -- it opens on empty shelves and fills them when the accounts arrive. 44 assertions over six drives, including a purse of exactly 100, a call that throws, a catalogue of nothing, a cold open with no accounts, and a 24-second canary that proves no clock re-dresses the statue while you walk.

subtasks.text: The shop: your four design calls from the 10-27 readers (the reel, no repeats in Open 5, the statue, what a case is worth)
subtasks.note: TWO OF THE FOUR ARE LIVE on the real domain; the other two need a database change and the Supabase token on this machine has expired, so the SQL is written, reviewed and waiting rather than half-applied. LIVE NOW. (1) The case reel settles in 4 seconds instead of 6.2, and five at once in 5.2 instead of 7.9. Reveal now stays on the bar. (2) Under the odds, the case finally says what it is worth TO YOU: how many of its skins you have still to find, and the real chance the next one is new. That second number is the point -- owning two thirds of a case and having a two-thirds chance of something new are different things, and the one that matters is the chance, which is the chance of the tiers you are actually missing. It is worked out from the live list and your own locker, so nothing in it can go stale. A guest is told the size of the case instead; somebody who has every skin is told so, with the number; and if the odds table will not load the count still stands and NO percentage is invented -- a 0% there would be the worst lie the screen could tell. WAITING ON THE TOKEN. (3) Open 5 cannot hand you the same skin twice: each draw is told what the others already took. The outside readers found a real hole in my first version of this -- the way I passed that list could have been sent BY A BROWSER, which would have let anyone name their own prize and buy a Divine for 100 tickets. Rewritten so the browser cannot reach it at all. (4) The plaza statue becomes a real player's showcase: the last person to pull an epic or better, wearing their skin, with their name on a plaque on the base. The arcade side of it is live and tested -- the room asks for the name, and when there is nobody to show it falls back to the catalogue rotation exactly as it does today, so nothing looks broken in the meantime. It lights up the moment the database read is applied. One decision for you, in the report.

subtasks.text: The shop rack: the good skins first, and a phone that shows a whole row of them
subtasks.note: LIVE on the real domain, 61 checks green there. The rack used to open on seventeen grey Commons and work up; it opens on Divine now and works down, so the first thing a stranger scrolls into is dragons and seraphs. On a phone that was not enough on its own: the Arcade Case strip was 215 pixels of an 844-pixel screen -- a two-line title, a three-line tagline and a row of five little portraits -- and it pushed the first row of skins clean off the bottom. The tagline and the portraits are both said again inside the case screen, one tap away on the same strip, so on a phone they are gone and the strip is 80 pixels. The rack also takes 58% of a phone instead of 52%. A whole row of cards now ends above the fold with its price tag on it, which matters because of the next line. Worth saying: my own check passed this at first with the row head 39 pixels from the bottom edge and nothing else visible -- a pass that was a lie, and the bar is now a whole card row, measured.

subtasks.text: The shop: buy four named skins outright instead of only opening cases
subtasks.note: LIVE, proven on the site 10-30. You renewed the key on the 29th; this is the walk that proved the shop actually behaves. The Duck Floatie bought off the shelf for 80 tickets with the test account, and an Open 5 gave five DIFFERENT skins with no shelf skin among them -- so you can never pay for the Diver and pull it out of a case ten minutes later. The statue in the plaza wears the last big pull with the name painted on its base. Older note, kept: BUILT AND VERIFIED, BUT DARK: it needs one database command and the Supabase token on this machine has returned 'invalid access token' since the 26th. Renew it and the shop lights up with no new build -- the shelf is drawn from the database rows, so the moment the four rows exist the shop has a shelf, and until then it is exactly the shop you have today. That is the whole design and the first third of the check exists to prove it: with no rows, no shelf section, no price on any card, and the case screen still calls itself the only way to get a skin. With the rows: Duck Floatie 80, Bumble Bee 150, Gumball Machine 260, Deep-Sea Diver 450, pinned above the rack with their prices on the cards, a Buy button that takes the tickets, and the four taken OUT of the case pool so you can never pay 450 for the Diver and pull it out of a 100-ticket case ten minutes later. The copy that the shelf makes untrue -- 'every skin comes from the Arcade Case', 'the only way to get a skin' -- is rewritten to count both sides instead of claiming either, so whichever is true today is what the screen says. The database half (the four prices, the buy routine rebuilt as a four-name allowlist so a browser can never name its own price, and the case draw taught to skip them) is written, reviewed and waiting in one file.

subtasks.text: Two outside readers went over Toy Fury line by line (10-27) and found nine things
subtasks.note: FIVE OF THE NINE ARE LIVE on the real domain; the other four are edits to the arcade room file, which another lane was writing at the same moment, so they stay queued rather than being fought over. What shipped. (1) THE BIGGEST ONE: a race used to tell you what it was for ONE SECOND -- the rule flashed up and the countdown painted over it -- so nobody ever learned what they were racing for, what their car was standing on, or that losing it was permanent. The grid now HOLDS on a card until you ask for the lights: the room, the rule it dealt and how hard the field is, your car and its panels, which slot of how many you start in, the laps, the coin it cost, that finishing pays 3 tickets and beating a bot pays more, and that losing every panel loses the car for good -- then PRESS DRIFT. Every line is READ off the race that was just built, not typed into a label, and on a phone it says 'tap ITEM', because the old line named a key a phone has not got. (2) The tutorial's first step is now what WINS this race, taken from the rule that was dealt -- on a Knockout deal it says 'last place is out every lap', which changes how you drive from the first corner. It used to be the SIXTH step, after five steps of controls. (3) A wreck was marked on your phone and then fired at the server with the answer thrown away: if that write failed, the permadeath simply did not happen -- the next visit to the garage re-read the server and handed the car back. The loss is written down before the call now, retried, retried again every time the garage opens, and the car stays gone on your device in the meantime. (4) A race could start on a car the server had never heard of (it quietly handed you a kart with no record), which meant no panels carried in and no wreck could ever be recorded -- it refuses now and tells you the starter is free. (5) The repair bill was priced two different ways on two screens for the same car; both now use the server's own price list and its own arithmetic. Checked by 30 assertions in a new file, including a stand-in server that REFUSES the wreck and then throws, so the retry is proven against failure rather than against a server that always says yes; photographed on a phone, a phone turned sideways and a desk, and the card was moved up off the middle of the screen because the first desk shot had it written straight across the car it was describing.

subtasks.text: Two outside readers went over the tavern line by line (10-27) and found eleven things
subtasks.note: ALL ELEVEN ARE LIVE on the real domain, and one of them was not a bug (the readers asked for a button label that has been there since the table was built -- it is asserted now so it stays). The worst one was money: the PINBALL took your coin the instant the machine opened and settled a loss when you walked off, so walking up to read the glass and stepping away cost you a go and paid you nothing. The coin is for the LAUNCH now -- the panel says '1 coin when you launch' before it charges anything, a guest is told it is free instead of being billed for a coin they have not got, and a leave before the plunge spends and settles nothing. Second worst, and it is on every hold-to-act button in the tavern: a thumb that drifted a few pixels off the button fired what it was winding up. At the pool table that SHOT the cue at whatever power the meter was at, at the oche it threw the dart mid-steady, at pinball it dropped the flipper you were holding up and fired the plunger early. The buttons keep your finger now until you actually lift it. Third: the jukebox remembered a single failed fetch for the rest of the session -- it said 'try again in a minute' and never tried, for ever. Fourth: darts had exactly one end-of-game ceremony (the rating -- bar legend, sharpshooter) and it could never run, because it sat behind a test no live game has ever passed; it fires at the end of a Rusty match now, and the chalkboard's BEST has moved off 0 for the first time and is kept between sittings. The rest is copy that was lying: the pool table's only control hint was for a mouse, so a phone was told nothing; darts never explained the HOT number or the bull round anywhere on screen and now has a line that does not move; the DARTS sign said 'three darts' for a five-round game; the jukebox promised 'everyone in the tavern hears it' to a player standing alone; a full queue said nothing at all; and walking out of a friend's pool game now tells you they keep the table and the house picks up your cue, which is exactly what their screen has always said. 83 assertions, on a desk, on a real phone, and across two arcades in one room over the live relay -- including the coin, checked on the real call path with a stand-in bank that records instead of spending.

subtasks.text: Two outside readers went over Strike City line by line (10-27) and found ten things
subtasks.note: ALL TEN ARE LIVE on the real domain. Strike City is the only game anybody has ever played for ten minutes, so this one was worth doing properly. The first frame: your ball starts on the return behind you, and nothing told a stranger to turn round -- there is an arrow on it now that rides the edge of the screen while it is out of sight, so the arrow IS the way to turn, and the how-to's first step stays lit with everything you cannot do yet stepped back out of the way. The sheet now carries what you are chasing: the target, what is settled, what is still owed on an open strike or spare, and the best this game can still finish at. That last number is the honest one -- a simple 'are you on pace' line would call an unresolved strike BEHIND, which is backwards, so it works out the best score your real throws can still reach instead. Your own strike finally gets a moment: the lens tightens for a fifth of a second and the lit wall over your pins flashes amber. No new sound, and nothing happens on anyone else's lane or on the island's show lane -- the ears rule from the 15th. Three lines that teach, once a game each: the first time you face a part-cleared rack, your first mark, and the turn your own line has actually dried out (measured off the oil, not guessed). With friends: a turn now runs out after 25 seconds with the last ten counted out loud, so somebody wandering off to the bar can no longer freeze the lane -- and only one screen is allowed to end a turn, which is what stops the four games drifting apart. A tie is announced as a tie with the number (it used to hand one of them a loss); 'bowl solo instead' takes you to a free lane instead of printing advice and leaving you waiting; the rematch button says it rematches this group, and it can no longer open on somebody who walked out. The shoe counter has stopped promising a free game it cannot give -- the price is said once, where the coin is actually taken. Last, and it came out of recording a whole game on a phone: turned SIDEWAYS, the how-to was a 132-pixel letterbox over 424 pixels of card, cut off mid-sentence, with the swipe diagrams, step four and the Got it button all below a fold nobody would guess was there. It is a two-column card now and every word of it is on the glass. 36 checks on a desk and a phone, each with a canary that proves it can fail, plus a whole ten-frame game bowled upright and sideways, and two real arcades bowling together in one room.

subtasks.text: Strike City: your three calls from the 10-27 readers (the scores to beat, the shoes, the ball return)
subtasks.note: ALL THREE ARE LIVE on the real domain, 10-28. (1) THE SCORES TO BEAT ARE 90 / 120 / 150 / 180, down from 90 / 130 / 170 / 220. The old ladder was made up rather than measured, and it mattered: 220 is roughly what a league bowler averages and 170 is a good night, so three of the four buttons were selling a prize nobody in that room could actually win. The new rungs are thirty apart, about one open frame each, and the number is marked in the file to be retuned off real finished games once strangers have bowled some -- not off another guess. (2) THE LANE HANDS YOU THE SHOES. Walking straight at the lanes is what the room's own view invites you to do, and pressing the button there used to answer 'no -- go and rent shoes first', which is the worst possible first word to a stranger. It puts the rentals on for you now and says so. Nothing was taken away: your figure still visibly changes its boots, the rentals still come off when you leave the alley, and the counter by the door still rents to anyone who walks over to it. (3) THE BALL RETURN RITUAL IS KEPT, deliberately -- your first ball still waits on the return behind you and you still go and get it, which was your own call on 09-27. It now has its own written check so a later pass cannot quietly drop it. Also fixed, and only the screenshot found it: on a first visit the one longer button label was wide enough to push its neighbour out of shape and then spill its own text off both ends of the pill. The pool and darts pickers share that layout and had the same hole. 44 checks on a desk and a phone, every number read off the buttons a player actually sees rather than off the list in the code, and all 44 re-run against the live domain.

subtasks.text: Two outside readers went over the Undercroft line by line (10-27) and found eleven things
subtasks.note: ALL ELEVEN ARE LIVE on the real domain. Two of them are the first ten minutes of the game, and both were bad. (1) A brand-new player used to be met by a bookkeeping screen -- one card reading 'KNIGHT, LEVEL 1, no points spent yet' with RENAME, REMOVE and + NEW BUILD beside it, and not one word about what a knight actually IS. It is five job cards now, each with that job's own sentence, one click to walk in, and on a phone it is five rows that all fit the screen instead of a grid 1,097 pixels tall against 844 pixels of phone. Anyone who has already earned a badge or levelled anything gets the old screen, untouched. (2) The moment you win the bronze badge, the guildmaster says 'the board on the left wall is yours now' -- and the game turned you to face a blank wall 64 degrees away from it. Measured: the board was off the edge of the screen; it is dead centre now. (3) Dying used to be a red flash and a toast, both gone in a breath. It is a card you close yourself: what it spent, what went unpaid, and -- the half that was never said anywhere -- what you KEPT, with your real ember count and your finished contracts in it. It also shows up for a death the game cannot blame on anything, which used to skip the only line that explained anything. (4) On a phone, the three skill buttons you have not unlocked yet now leave the corner during a fight and come back after it. (5) The lesson cards counted FRAMES, not seconds, so on a fast screen an 11-second card was gone in 4. (6) The 'time in the dark' clock counted time spent in the guild hall and time spent on the victory screen. (7) In a room, a friend whose first instruction got lost dropped into a SOLO guild hall while the room still had them in the party; the host answers a second ask now instead of staying silent. Plus dead code deleted, and copy that was lying: it said the party leader pays everybody's coin (each pays their own) and it sent you to the trainer for a badge only the guildmaster gives. 47 assertions on a desk and a real phone, each written so it fails on the old build, with a deliberate false version run first on every leg that checks a state rather than a change -- plus 14 more on the room's own wiring. Re-run against the live domain, not the bundle.

subtasks.text: Undercroft, your five calls from 10-27: the first hall, a retry, banked skulls, a clean time, and a party in another dungeon
subtasks.note: ALL FIVE ARE LIVE on the real domain. (1) THE FIRST HALL. Four of four strangers died in it, and it is the first room anybody sees: two soldiers and an archer were all awake the moment you stepped off the stairs, with two of them off the side of the screen. It is one soldier at the door now, and the other two wake when you walk into the room. Worth saying plainly, because it changed the answer: the readers both named a 16-metre number as the distance a foe wakes at, and it is not one -- it only says whether a fight is already on. The real numbers are 13 metres for a soldier and 18 for an archer, and measured against those, the exact move both readers prescribed would have left all three awake at the door anyway. Same three foes, same damage, same health; three letters moved on the map. (2) THE ARCHER HAD NO TELL, and it was the one shot in the game that can reach you from off the screen: its arrow flies 18 metres and both its warnings were switched off past 14 and 16. They reach as far as the arrow now, and the whole edge of the screen on the archer's side washes amber -- the little arrow we had was 26 pixels on a 390-pixel phone, which is not a warning you can feel. A second bug in the same place meant a foe with no weapon drawn on the model warned you silently too. (3) ONE RETRY. Light a flame down there and your first death puts you back at it, with the contract still yours -- once per contract, not in the boss fight. The coin is still spent: it is a second chance, not a refund. The flames have saved nobody until today -- the game wrote down which one you lit and then never read it. (4) SKULLS CARRY OVER. Get three of six and die and the next go starts at three. Kill contracts only -- a boss contract and a 'not a drop from your flask' one are single runs by their own terms. (5) EVERY CONTRACT KEEPS YOUR BEST TIME AND A CLEAN MARK (no flask, no falling), on the pinned notice, on the sheet in your hands, in the list, and on the card when you finish. (6) AND A PARTY CAN NOW TAKE A CONTRACT IN ANOTHER DUNGEON -- before, a party was locked to whichever one it started in, for ever. The leader takes it and everyone goes. What stopped it was a single line, and the reason written beside it had not been true for weeks. 51 checks on a desk and a real phone, every behaviour one written so it fails on yesterday's build, and re-run against the live domain.

subtasks.text: Skate: friends feel present, and RUN IT BACK on the session end card
subtasks.note: SHIPPED 2026-10-23, live and re-checked on the domain with two real browsers in one room. Five things. subtasks.text: Skate sounds that tell the truth
