subtasks.text: The toy house deep dive: trims that clip in the corners, floating chairs, flicker, and enter a track from any side (Zack, 2026-10-28)
subtasks.note: 10-28 LIVE. The flicker in the corners was the four corner posts. Each was a white post exactly as deep as the brown skirting, so at every corner the post's faces sat in the SAME plane as the trim's -- white against brown at one depth, which is the flashing you see -- and it cut the brown band dead at each corner. The bottom of each post is now brown trim and the white starts above it, both standing 4 cm proud, so the band wraps the corner and nothing shares a plane. Measured, not guessed: a detector that re-renders one frame with the lens nudged a third of a millimetre forward read 24 flickering blocks dead centre of the old corner and 0 on the new one, with a deliberately planted fight reading 628 so I know it can see one. The door frames also stood 2 cm BEHIND the skirting that runs into them, so the brown band ended in mid-air; they are the proudest trim now. Tracks: you could only step into one from its stand -- measured at eight bearings round all eight mats, it was ONE side in eight. Now it is eight in eight: if you are close to a mat, from any side, you can hop in. The house also had real floating furniture -- four playroom stools with a seat and nothing underneath, the porch rocking chair hanging 33 cm over its own rails, the study armchair with no legs at all -- plus a bookcase that was a solid block with its thirty books buried inside it, teepee poles through the ceiling, and seven small things hovering over the shelf they sit on. All fixed, and the two bare halls now have a console and lamp, a bench, a tall clock, packing boxes, a coat rail, a laundry basket and a key shelf. Four floors that LOOKED like they should flicker were measured and do not, so they were left alone. Try: walk into the playroom corner, then walk at any track mat from the back.

subtasks.text: A clipping skill and a sweep: catch two surfaces fighting before they ship, then fix every one in the arcade (Zack, 2026-10-28)
subtasks.note: 10-29 LIVE, every room: 24 fights found, 24 fixed, none left, six updates all checked on the real site. The checker is built and the bowling alley is swept. The checker plants a fake flicker on purpose and has to catch it, on a desk and on a phone, and it goes red when the fake is taken away -- so when it says a wall is clean, that means something. It also pushes a planted flicker through the full decision path, because a checker that can never say yes would quietly report the whole arcade clean. Then I measured how far a detail has to stand off its surface before it stops fighting: a flat 1 mm clears every distance and angle I tested, so the house rule is 2 mm, and 4 mm where it is free. Two surprises, both written down: two surfaces dead flat-on to you do NOT flicker -- it takes an angle -- and the gap does not need to grow with distance, which is what everyone assumes. The flicker you saw by the bowling lanes was every neon sign in the arcade: the glowing tube was sized to land exactly on the edge of its own backing board, so the sign's EDGES crawled while its face looked fine. The board is 4 mm wider all round now and the lit tube has not moved a hair. The red glow round the EXIT door was dead flush with the door frame too. Bowling alley before: 4 proven fights. After: none, with the checker's own alarms still ringing. The hall is swept and live too -- four more, and the worst of them was the glowing stand-here ring at the shop lying dead flush with the lit floor it sits on, right where the room tells you to stand. The other two were the skee-ball lane: its cage posts shared a face with the booth wall, and the outer planks ran exactly to the edge of the bed under them, so both long edges of the lane crawled. Hall before: 4 fights in 281 places checked. After: none in 275, and I re-checked the whole island rather than just the four, so I know the fixes did not start a new one. The main plaza and the gate islands are swept and live as well, and that is where the worst one in the whole building was: the arcade's own front door. The swirling purple portal you walk into was being shredded into black wedges, because the dark panel it stands in sat at exactly the same depth as the swirl. It reads as a clean spiral now. The panel moved back 4 mm, not the swirl -- I tried moving the swirl first and the after-picture showed it had vanished behind the door entirely, which is exactly why I take a picture of every fix. Four more there: the jukebox's dark backing, the record labels in its dome, the neon outline round the plaza signs, and the rails on the race ribbon. Plaza before: 7 fights in 202 places. After: none in 146. The tavern is swept and live too, and it taught me the most. Only one thing there shared a plane -- the gold rail round the bar wall and the dark panelling under it -- and when I fixed it the picture came out EXACTLY the same, down to the pixel. The speckle I could see along that rail was never the two surfaces fighting; it was the rail's own thin edge shimmering, which is a different problem and not one you fix by moving anything. The checker now refuses to judge any strip too thin to have a middle, and says so instead of guessing. I kept the rail fix because the two really were sharing a plane, but I am not calling it a win you can see. The one thing the plan predicted would be worst in that room -- the glow on the tavern floor -- turned out to be clean. The skate park and the toy house came back clean -- nothing fighting in either, with the checker's alarms proving it was actually looking. Then I swept all six island gates one at a time, because sweeping from the middle of the arcade only reaches 60 m and the gates sit further out than that: 506 spots, one hit, and it was the bowling trophy -- its gold cap was dead level with the brown block it stands on, right across the top. That one I will say plainly: I could not get a before-and-after picture of it, because the camera lands in empty space at that exact spot. The fix rests on the numbers (two faces at the identical height) and a clean re-check, not on a photo, and I would rather tell you that than dress it up. Last room was the dungeon, which needed a checker of its own because it is a separate page. Seven fights there, and they came down to two lines: the big timbers on the guild hall's end walls were set exactly flush with the plaster behind them, and the archery targets had all three painted rings and the straw behind them at one single depth -- four colours arguing over every ring. The targets read clean now; the cream ring used to come out muddy and half-eaten. Dungeon before: 7 in 59 places. After: none in 47. One honest gap left: there are 238 more places in the arcade where two surfaces really do share a plane, but every one is a strip too narrow on screen for the checker to judge fairly -- trims, kerbs, mouldings. They are all written down and want judging by their numbers rather than by eye, and the toy house's share of them belongs with the dressing job already on your list. Also: the new rule is written up as a skill but not switched on yet -- that is your call, and the note for it is waiting. Try: walk at the arcade's front door and look at the purple swirl, then the archery targets in the guild hall, then the ball-weight sign down the bowling lanes.

subtasks.text: The lobby, made consistent: arches over every bridge, jump pads, the rope to Stardust, and the blank gold plaque (Zack, 2026-10-28)
subtasks.note: Live 10-29. Your count was exact: one arch over six doorways, and a jump pad on four of the six bridges. The whole room now runs on one sentence -- a bridge is walked, a gap is jumped. Every doorway has the same lit arch over it, including the two corner ones that the old code could not have reached at all, and each sign names where it goes in the words of the door at the far end, so an arch can never promise something the door does not say. No bridge has a jump pad on it any more: there were sixteen pads, there are eight, and the eight that went are exactly the eight that stood in the middle of a walk. Every pad you jump between islands with is untouched -- those are the only way across where no bridge runs, so losing one would have stranded you. Where each bridge lands there is now the brass doorstep with two lamps that only the two corner islands used to get. The little rope with the gold ball on the way to the Stardust Tavern is gone: it was two four-post fragments standing in the middle of the red carpet fencing nothing, in a fatter post than the rope round the edge of the room twelve metres behind it. The rope round the lip stays and so does the velvet queue into the arcade, because those two are patterns, not leftovers. The blank gold plaque on the shop stand now reads SKINS & CASES, and underneath, spend your tickets here -- painted into the plaque itself rather than hung in front of it, so there is nothing to flicker and it costs nothing to draw. It does not just repeat THE SHOP, because the sign hanging eight metres over your head already says that. One thing worth knowing: six arches put the room over its own speed budget on two islands, so rather than raise the budget I made the little bulbs cheaper to draw -- they are twelve-centimetre balls seen from ten metres and more, and zoomed in four times against the old ones they are the same picture. Walk out of any door and look up. Added 10-29, live: one of those jump pads was half blocked and nobody had noticed. On the racing island the pit counter and its safety rail overran the pad you hop to the bowling island from -- the counter's end even hung over the pad's edge in mid-air -- so standing on that corner shoved you a metre back off it. The whole pit row moved two metres up the lane, counter, garages and tyres together, and the pad is open ground now. Measured on the live site, not just here.

subtasks.text: Strike City: real bowling at the shoe desk -- party size, everyone pays for shoes, a ball each, the ball return, pay per game (Zack, 2026-10-28)
subtasks.note: LIVE on the real domain, 10-29, in four deploys. Walk into the alley and a little card pops up with the four steps -- desk, ball rack, your lane, back to the desk for more. It does not stop you walking while you read it. The shoe guy has a name now and he talks: he asks how many are bowling (just you, 2, 3 or 4), then how many games, then shows the price and tells you which lane you are on. That is one conversation, not a menu. The shoes cost a coin and that coin IS your first game -- one charge, not two -- and the lane will not take you barefoot any more, it sends you to the desk and lights up step one of the card. Every game after the first costs its own coin, and you buy them at the desk, not by picking up a ball. If the till says no you get no shoes and no lane, and it tells you why. Then the ball: the rack is a proper screen with the five weights and what each one does, and the weight is real -- the same throw with an 8 and with a 16 leaves different pins on nine of eighteen lines I measured. You carry the ball in your hand across the room and press E at the ball return to drop it in, and the lane will not take you until you have. Every bowler in your party has their own ball sitting in that return, in the colour of its weight, so with two of you booked you really do see two balls in it. With friends: say 2 of us and you land on your friend's lane automatically, and the lane WAITS for the party you booked -- a three that only has two seated never starts, which it used to do after eight seconds, leaving the third standing at the ball rack. Proved with two real browsers over thirty samples. The table and stool that stood in the walk from the door to the desk are moved aside; I measured it, they sat dead on the line. A bug worth naming: every friend's ball was being re-rolled at 12 lb on your screen whatever they picked, so your screens disagreed about the pins -- that is fixed. And the clipping at the ends: nine places where two surfaces shared exactly the same plane are fixed, including the seam at the far end of every lane and the four top corners of the room. One thing I left: the price says 2 coins, not 1. The database row that changes it is written and sitting there, but the database key is still dead, so it will read 2 until that key comes back -- nothing else needs touching when it does.

subtasks.text: Strike City: tickets for how well you bowl, and three ways to play -- solo, friends, and wager bowl, winner takes all (Zack, 2026-10-28)
subtasks.note: ALL THREE WAYS ARE LIVE on the real domain, 10-29, and your key renewal at lunchtime is what switched the first two on. Solo and friends: the alley pays you for the game you bowled -- every strike 3 tickets, every spare 2, every tidy nine 1 -- and the score sheet grows a green strip under your own row showing what each frame earned. No more 'beat 120 to win'. Everyone bowling together earns their own card that way. A game costs 1 coin now, not 2. WAGER BOWL, which is the part that was still missing this morning: at the shoe desk, after you say how many are bowling and how many games, whoever made the room is asked what the lane is playing for -- nothing, 5, 10, 25 or 50 tickets each. The sheet names the pot for your party on every button and will not offer you a number bigger than the tickets you actually have. Everyone then pays their own coin at the desk and puts their own tickets up, and the till says the number back to you before you pay, whether you set it or your friend did; if you cannot cover it you are told plainly that you bowl this one for nothing rather than being quietly left out. Best score takes the pot. ONE THING TO DECIDE, in the briefing: a tie splits the pot between everyone level at the top. That is what the server already does for every other game that plays for tickets, so I shipped it and said it out loud on the sheet -- 'Winner takes the pot. A tie splits it.' -- but the rule is yours to keep or change. Two honest limits: nobody has played a real wager yet with two phones in one room, and once you leave the desk nothing in the alley reminds you there is a pot on the lane. Both are written down as the next jobs. 10-29, live: a follow-up off this row is fixed too -- the amber YOUR BALL arrow that points at your ball on the return was landing on top of the lane panel, so on a phone it covered the 'How to bowl' link and stacked its own two words into an unreadable pile, and sideways it sat across the control line. It now stops at the top of the panel and stays on one line. Worth saying plainly: the job as written blamed the panel's header and asked me to rebuild it, and that was the wrong thing -- the header was fine, the arrow was the thing in the way, and rebuilding the header would have changed nothing.

subtasks.text: Take Dark Room, Tow Truck and Deep Line off the floor (Zack, 2026-10-29)
subtasks.note: LIVE on the real domain, 10-29. All three cabinets are gone from the arcade floor and from the All Games list. Nothing was deleted: the three pages still open if you have a link, and putting any of them back is one line. The room rebuilt itself round the gap -- the floor sign reads 22 machines now instead of 25, and the hall is one row shorter, so there is less empty carpet to walk. Checked by walking in on a desk screen and on a phone: no errors either way, and the speed check passed with room to spare (the hall draws less than it did). The three names still sit in some of the lists that say how a game should fill a phone screen; those are only read when you open that game, so they do nothing now and removing them would have been a bigger change than leaving them.

subtasks.text: The flicker around every cabinet screen in the arcade (Zack, 2026-10-29)
subtasks.note: LIVE on the real domain, 10-29. You were right about the cause -- two pieces of material sitting on exactly the same plane, so the machine had no way to decide which one was in front and picked a different answer as you walked. Two places, and both of them were shared by every cabinet in the room, which is why you saw it on all of them: the thin blue glow around the picture started on the very same line the dark frame started on, and the lit bar across the marquee ended on the very same line as the metal cap at each end of it. The glow now laps 3mm over the edge of the picture, the way a real screen surround does, and the cap now wraps its bar instead of stopping level with it. Nothing else moved. Measured rather than guessed: I walked the hall thirteen times, once with every cabinet wearing each of the thirteen different machine styles, and counted every pair of surfaces sharing a plane near a screen -- 1732 of them before, none after. The room's other numbers fell by exactly that same 1732, which is how I know I did not quietly break something else while fixing this. I also photographed one cabinet from a sharp side-on angle and nudged the camera a hair, which is what makes a flicker show itself: nine flickering patches before, zero after, and the before picture put them exactly where you said -- the marquee bar, its end caps, and the left and bottom edge of the picture. Go stand close to any machine and walk slowly past it.
